articles.title: Show DEV: Beating the Browser Memory Ceiling — Streaming 50GB WebRTC Files Direct-to-Disk with OPFS (Part 3)
articles.description: Sender backpressure is only half the battle. Here is how I solved the receiver-side memory trap in WebRTC, streaming 50GB+ files to mobile Safari and Chrome without blowing the 1.5GB RAM ceiling.
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

🚀 Live Web App (Free, Zero Signup): air-stream.pages.dev

⭐ GitHub Repo (MIT): github.com/QuantumTechCoder/AirStream

📖 The Series So Far:

  • Part 1: AirStream — Stream Gigabytes Browser-to-Browser with WebRTC
  • Part 2: Monetizing an Open Source WebRTC App Without Stripe or Subscriptions

The Hidden Trap of WebRTC File Transfers

If you read any WebRTC file transfer tutorial online, you'll see people celebrate Backpressure Control:
"Just monitor dataChannel.bufferedAmount! If the buffer exceeds 1MB, pause file slicing until onbufferedamountlow triggers. Boom, zero RAM crashes on the sender!"

And that works brilliantly... for the sender.

The sender simply reads a 64KB slice from disk via file.slice(), ships it down the socket, and lets the garbage collector discard it. The sender's RAM never exceeds 30MB, even when transferring a 100GB disk image.

But what happens on the receiving device?

Almost every WebRTC app on GitHub handles incoming chunks like this:

// The Classic WebRTC Receiver Trap 
const incomingChunks: Uint8Array[] = [];

dataChannel.onmessage = (event) => {
  incomingChunks.push(new Uint8Array(event.data)); // Storing raw chunks in RAM!

  if (receivedBytes >= totalBytes) {
    // Attempting to assemble 10GB into a single JavaScript Blob
    const fileBlob = new Blob(incomingChunks);
    const downloadUrl = URL.createObjectURL(fileBlob);
  }
};

On a developer workstation with 32GB or 64GB of DDR5 RAM, sending a 4GB or 5GB video across a gigabit local Wi-Fi router works without a hitch. You test it, high-five yourself, and deploy to production.

Then a user opens the app on their iPhone (Safari) or Android phone (Chrome) to receive a 10GB video.

At 1.4GB received, the browser tab freezes. Two seconds later:

"A problem repeatedly occurred with this webpage." (Safari)

"Aw, Snap! Out of Memory." (Chrome)

The tab was assassinated by the mobile OS kernel.

The Anatomy of the Mobile Memory Ceiling

Why do mobile browsers crash so aggressively on large transfers?

  1. Per-Tab Heap Quotas: On iOS WebKit (which powers every browser on iOS, including Chrome and Firefox for iOS), the operating system enforces an aggressive per-process memory limit. Depending on the device model, tabs that cross ~1.2GB to 1.8GB of RAM are instantly terminated via SIGKILL. Android Chrome enforces similar per-tab process memory caps.
  2. The "Blob Assembly Spike": When you hold 80,000 distinct Uint8Array chunk references in a JavaScript array, the V8/JavaScriptCore garbage collector cannot free a single byte. Worse, when you call new Blob(incomingChunks), the browser momentarily doubles the memory overhead while constructing the internal blob descriptor structure.
  3. Double Buffering: Creating URL.createObjectURL(blob) keeps the entire file pinned in browser heap storage until the tab is closed or URL.revokeObjectURL() is called.

If AirStream's motto is "Stream Gigabytes Browser-to-Browser with Zero Limits", crashing on 10GB transfers to phones was completely unacceptable.

We needed a way to stream incoming 64KB WebRTC packets directly to the device's storage disk in real time, completely bypassing the JavaScript heap.

The Progressive Direct-to-Disk Architecture

To solve this across all major platforms, I engineered a 3-tier progressive storage engine:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               Incoming 64KB WebRTC Chunk               │
└───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                            │
            Does browser support Disk Streaming?
                            │
            ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
       Yes (Chrome/Edge)             Yes (iOS Safari, Firefox)
            │                               │
            ▼                               ▼
 ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ Tier 1: FSA Engine   │        │ Tier 2: OPFS Sandbox │
 │ showSaveFilePicker() │        │ navigator.storage    │
 │ -> createWritable()  │        │ -> createWritable()  │
 └──────────┬───────────┘        └──────────┬───────────┘
            │                               │
            ▼                               ▼
  Saved directly to OS disk       Streamed into device sandbox
   RAM Usage: < 20MB               RAM Usage: < 25MB

Tier 1: File System Access API (Chromium / Desktop)

In Chromium browsers (Chrome, Edge, Opera), the W3C File System Access API allows web apps to stream bytes directly into a file handle chosen by the user:

// When the incoming transfer starts:
const fileHandle = await window.showSaveFilePicker({
  suggestedName: meta.name,
});
const writable = await fileHandle.createWritable();

// As each 64KB WebRTC chunk arrives:
await writable.write(chunkPayload);

// When transfer completes:
await writable.close();
// Done! The file is already on the user's hard drive!

The Benefit:

  • Zero RAM Consumption: As soon as writable.write(chunkPayload) executes, the bytes are flushed to the OS filesystem cache. The 64KB buffer is immediately garbage collected.
  • Zero Download Delay: The file doesn't need to be "downloaded" at the end. Once the progress bar hits 100%, the file is already sitting in their Downloads or Documents folder, completely written!

Tier 2: Origin Private File System (OPFS — Safari & Mobile)

The File System Access API is fantastic, but what about iOS Safari, macOS Safari, and Firefox where showSaveFilePicker is not supported?

Enter the Origin Private File System (OPFS).

OPFS provides a private, sandboxed, highly-optimized filesystem accessible via navigator.storage.getDirectory(). It is fully supported in iOS Safari 15.2+, Safari 17+, Chrome, and Firefox!

Crucially: OPFS requires zero permission prompts or user gestures.

Here is how AirStream automatically routes chunks to OPFS when receiving files $\ge$ 50MB:

// src/core/transfer/DiskStreamWriter.ts
export async function createDiskStreamWriter(
  fileId: string,
  _fileName: string,
  fileType: string,
  fileSize: number,
  preferredFsaHandle?: any
): Promise<DiskWriter> {
  // If user on Chrome picked a destination folder
  if (preferredFsaHandle?.createWritable) {
    const writable = await preferredFsaHandle.createWritable();
    return {
      storageMode: 'fsa',
      write: (chunk) => writable.write(chunk),
      close: async () => {
        await writable.close();
        return { savedToDisk: true };
      },
      abort: () => writable.abort(),
    };
  }

  // Automatic OPFS Sandbox on iOS Safari & modern browsers (files >= 50MB)
  if (isOpfsSupported() && fileSize >= 50 * 1024 * 1024) {
    const root = await navigator.storage.getDirectory();
    const tempFileName = `airstream_${fileId}.tmp`;
    const fileHandle = await root.getFileHandle(tempFileName, { create: true });

    if (typeof (fileHandle as any).createWritable === 'function') {
      const writable = await (fileHandle as any).createWritable();

      return {
        storageMode: 'opfs',
        write: (chunk) => writable.write(chunk),
        close: async () => {
          await writable.close();
          // Access the disk-backed file handle
          const file = await fileHandle.getFile();
          // createObjectURL on an OPFS File does NOT allocate RAM!
          const downloadUrl = URL.createObjectURL(file);
          return { downloadUrl, savedToDisk: false };
        },
        abort: async () => {
          await writable.abort().catch(() => {});
          await root.removeEntry(tempFileName).catch(() => {});
        },
      };
    }
  }

  // Tier 3: In-Memory Blob Fallback (for small files < 50MB)
  const chunks: Uint8Array[] = [];
  return {
    storageMode: 'ram',
    write: async (chunk) => { chunks.push(chunk); },
    close: async () => {
      const blob = new Blob(chunks, { type: fileType });
      chunks.length = 0;
      return { downloadUrl: URL.createObjectURL(blob), savedToDisk: false };
    },
    abort: async () => { chunks.length = 0; },
  };
}

Why OPFS is a Game Changer for Mobile:

When createObjectURL(file) is called on an OPFS-backed File object, the browser does not load the file into JavaScript RAM. The blob URL points directly to the sandbox file on disk. When the user taps "Save", the native mobile browser streams the bytes directly into the iOS Files app or Android Downloads folder!

Concurrency Challenge: The Sequential Write Queue

WebRTC DataChannels can receive packets at rates of 20MB/s to 100MB/s+ on local Wi-Fi. That means incoming chunks can arrive every 1 to 2 milliseconds.

File system writes (writable.write()) are asynchronous. If you call writable.write() concurrently before the previous chunk has flushed, the browser will throw an error:

"InvalidStateError: A write operation is already in progress."

To guarantee that chunks are written strictly in order without locking the thread or dropping packets, I implemented a Sequential Promise Queue:

// src/core/transfer/FileReceiver.ts
public handleChunk(packetBuffer: ArrayBuffer): void {
  // Decode framed header (chunk index, fileId)
  const payloadBytes = new Uint8Array(packetBuffer, 8 + fileIdLen);
  const active = this.activeTransfers.get(fileId);
  if (!active) return;

  // Chain writes sequentially onto a promise queue
  active.writeQueue = active.writeQueue
    .then(async () => {
      const writer = active.writer || (active.writer = await active.writerPromise);
      await writer.write(payloadBytes);
    })
    .catch((err) => {
      console.error('Error streaming chunk to disk:', err);
    });

  // Track progress metrics...
}

When the sender finishes, finalizeTransfer() simply waits for await active.writeQueue. Once every queued chunk has flushed to disk, writer.close() finalizes the stream.

The Results: Flat 20MB RAM at 50GB Scale

Here is what the receiver's memory profile looks like now during a stress test:

Transfer Size Old Receiver (In-Memory Blob) New Receiver (OPFS / FSA Direct)
500 MB ~600 MB Heap 18 MB Heap
2 GB ~2.4 GB Heap (Crashed iOS) 21 MB Heap (Flawless on iOS)
10 GB Instant Tab Crash 23 MB Heap
50 GB Impossible 24 MB Heap

Whether you transfer a 10MB PDF or a 50GB 8K ProRes video, the JavaScript heap stays rock-solid under 25MB.

Fuel the Dev (Tip Me a Coffee in USDC) ☕

Building open-source P2P software with zero telemetry, zero corporate sponsors, and zero ads takes a lot of late-night debugging.

If AirStream saved your workflow, eliminated a paid cloud storage subscription, or helped you stream huge files between your devices, consider fueling future development!

You can tap the Tip button directly on air-stream.pages.dev to send 1, 2, or 5 USDC on Base or Polygon (gas is < \$0.01!), or send directly to my EVM address:
0x2cef0473f985156eDe84312Ce0BeB94B602d26E4

Every micro-tip keeps AirStream independent, ad-free, and 100% open-source for everyone.

Let's Discuss!

  • Have you hit the per-tab memory ceiling on mobile Safari or Chrome with web apps before?
  • What are your favorite patterns for handling massive streams or files in client-side TypeScript?
  • What other browser storage quirks have you encountered when working with OPFS or File System Access?

Drop your thoughts below! 👇

articles.title: JavaScript told me to buy 8 bags of concrete. I needed 7.
articles.description: Open your browser console and paste this:    4 * 3 * (4 / 12) * 1.05 / 0.6        Enter fullscreen...
articles.body_html:
Open your browser console and paste this:

4 * 3 * (4 / 12) * 1.05 / 0.6

That's a small pad for an AC unit. 4 ft by 3 ft, 4 inches thick, plus 5% extra for spillage, divided by 0.6 cubic feet (what one 80 lb bag of concrete mix makes). On paper the answer is 7. Exactly 7 bags.

JavaScript says 7.000000000000001.

Every bag calculator rounds up, because nobody sells 0.4 of a bag. So you wrap it in Math.ceil() and the page tells you to buy 8.

One extra bag isn't a disaster. It's six bucks and 80 more pounds to drag across a parking lot. But I wanted to know how often it happens, so I brute-forced it.

How often does this actually happen?

I ran every slab from 1 x 1 ft up to 20 x 20 ft, at 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 inches thick, with 0, 5, 10 and 15% waste, for 40, 60 and 80 lb bags. That's 12,600 combinations.

2,179 of them work out to an exact whole number of bags. 620 of those come out one bag high with a plain Math.ceil. That's 28% of the cases where the math is clean.

These aren't weird edge cases either. 4 x 4 at 6 inches with 5% waste. 6 x 3 at 4 inches with 10%. The boring sizes people actually pour.

Here's the script if you want to check me:

let exact = 0, wrong = 0;
for (const bag of [0.6, 0.45, 0.3]) // 80, 60, 40 lb yields in cu ft
  for (let l = 1; l <= 20; l++)
    for (let w = 1; w <= l; w++)
      for (const inches of [2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
        for (const waste of [0, 5, 10, 15]) {
          const bags = l * w * (inches / 12) * (1 + waste / 100) / bag;
          if (Math.abs(bags - Math.round(bags)) < 1e-9) {
            exact++;
            if (Math.ceil(bags) !== Math.round(bags)) wrong++;
          }
        }
console.log({ exact, wrong }); // { exact: 2179, wrong: 620 }

The fix is four lines 

const EPSILON = 1e-9;

export function roundUp(value: number, step = 1): number {
  const steps = value / step;
  const snapped =
    Math.abs(steps - Math.round(steps)) < EPSILON ? Math.round(steps) : steps;
  return Math.ceil(snapped) * step;
}

If the number is within a billionth of a whole number, treat it as that whole number. Then round up. 7.000000000000001 becomes 7. 7.2 still becomes 8, which is correct, because 7.2 bags means you need 8.

The step argument came later. A lot of ready-mix suppliers sell by the half yard, so roundUp(2.1, 0.5) returns 2.5, which is what you'd actually order from the truck.

Is 1e-9 the "right" epsilon? Honestly, it's just way bigger than float noise at these magnitudes and way smaller than any real fraction of a bag. Nobody is pouring a slab where a billionth of a bag matters.

Bug two: toFixed doesn't round like a human

This one I knew about in theory and still walked into:

(1.005).toFixed(2)          // "1.00"
Math.round(1.005 * 100) / 100 // 1

1.005 can't be stored exactly. It's really something like 1.00499999999999989..., so both methods round it down. Correct for the computer. Wrong for the person reading it.

For money, that's a cent. For a calculator, it's worse than it sounds. While I was looking at existing concrete calculators before building mine, one of them showed 1.536 cubic yards in the big headline number and 1.556 a few lines lower, on the same result card. Same inputs. I don't know exactly how that happened on their end, but my guess is two parts of the page rounding the same value two different ways.

If you're about to order concrete and the page disagrees with itself, which number do you trust? You don't. You close the tab.

My fix was a small relative nudge before rounding:

export function roundTo(value: number, decimals: number): number {
  const factor = 10 ** decimals;
  const scaled = value * factor;
  const nudged = scaled + Math.sign(scaled) * Math.abs(scaled) * 1e-12;
  return Math.round(nudged) / factor;
}
// roundTo(1.005, 2) === 1.01

The function matters less than the rule I made around it: there's exactly one rounding module. The headline number, the little stat chips, the shopping list, the worked example in the article text, all of it calls the same functions. There's a test that asserts the headline equals the shopping list number for every tool. If two places can format a number differently, eventually they will, and it'll be in production.

Bug three: people type commas

US users type 1,250. A lot of other people type 0,5 and mean half. Both show up in the same input box.

The rule I ended up with: a comma is a decimal point, unless the string looks like a properly grouped thousands number.

const grouped = /^-?[1-9]\d{0,2}(,\d{3})+(\.\d+)?$/.test(trimmed);
const normalised = grouped
  ? trimmed.replace(/,/g, '')
  : trimmed.replace(/,/g, '.');

Note the [1-9] at the start. A leading zero never starts a thousands group, so 0,500 reads as half, not five hundred. That one came from a real test case that failed, not from me being clever.

The part that wasn't a bug: my mulch page was shipping drywall prices

The site is static Astro with Preact islands for the calculators. No framework runtime on the pages that don't need one.

Even so, my first build shipped 61 to 64 KB of gzipped JS per tool page. The culprit was data. Every page bundled the full prices and materials files: every gravel density, every bag yield, every paint coverage rate, for every tool. The mulch page was carrying drywall prices around.

The fix was more fun than I expected. At build time, each calculator gets driven like a bored visitor would drive it: every shape tab, both unit systems, every option in every dropdown, a second area, every waste chip, then a batch of random inputs. Every data entry the engine reads along the way gets recorded. Only those entries get written into the page.

Then a separate test runs a bigger, differently seeded batch of random inputs against just that slice and checks the results match the full data. If the build-time walk missed something, a test fails instead of a visitor's calculator.

Result: 36 to 38 KB per page, and Lighthouse mobile scores of 100 across the board on all 34 live pages. No Calculate button either. Results update as you type with a 150ms debounce, which felt obvious until I saw how many calculators still make you click.

What I'd tell anyone building a calculator

  • Never Math.ceil a float that came out of a division. Snap first.
  • One rounding module. Not a helper. The only place numbers become strings.
  • Write the hand-checked examples first. A 10 x 10 slab at 4 inches is 1.23 cubic yards, 56 bags of 80 lb mix, 75 bags of 60 lb. I worked those out on paper before the engine existed, and they're still in the test suite. It's at 1,775 tests now. Most of them are boring. That's kind of the point.
  • Show your sources. Bag yields come off the manufacturer's data sheet. Gravel density varies by supplier and moisture, so the field is editable and the page says so. People trust a number more when they can see where it came from.
  • Test at 390px wide. That's someone standing in a hardware store aisle with one hand free. A few calculators I looked at hide the shape preview on mobile, which is exactly where you need it.

Go try to break it

All of this lives in Gravel Calculator HQ, a free set of calculators for concrete, gravel, mulch, topsoil, drywall and paint. No sign-up, no pop-ups.

If you want to poke at the bag rounding, the concrete calculator has slab, footing, column, wall, steps, curb and circle tabs, and the share link puts your inputs in the URL so you can send me a bad result directly. The homepage is a gravel calculator that turns length, width and depth into cubic yards and tons, which is where the whole project started: one too many trips back to the supply yard for half a yard I didn't measure for.

If you can make any of them show NaN, Infinity, or a shopping list that disagrees with the headline, tell me in the comments. I'll fix it and credit you.

And I'm curious: what's the most expensive floating point bug you've shipped? Mine cost one bag of concrete. Feels like I got off easy.

articles.title: Claude Code `--resume` and Session Persistence in 2026: Picking Up Long Refactors Where You Left Off
articles.description: Learn when to resume Claude Code sessions versus starting fresh, how session state differs from conclusions, and the cost implications of long-running contexts in production workflows.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code --resume and Session Persistence in 2026: Picking Up Long Refactors Where You Left Off

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Claude Code sessions accumulate context with every turn, and developers reflexively reach for claude --resume to restore that investment. The --resume flag picks up an existing session by ID and continues where it left off, preserving the full conversation history. Past a certain threshold, that preserved history becomes a liability. Session length is proportional to noise, not signal. Resuming a long session floods the model with stale environment data and buries the decisions that matter.

The broken pattern treats session duration as an asset and resumes by default. Claude reads every tool call, every file edit, every approval prompt from the entire conversation. A session that ran for three hours re-reads three hours of context on every new turn. The first 90 minutes were exploratory work that led nowhere, but the cache read cost persists. The agent struggles to locate the one decision from turn 47 that still applies, and subtly undoes a fix from earlier in the session because the correction is buried in 200 prior messages.

A long session accumulates stale context, floods the model on resume, and buries live decisions in noise

The correct pattern distinguishes session state from session conclusions. Resume when the session holds unfinished work you cannot rebuild: a goal still in progress, a plan awaiting approval, or a permission mode set deliberately. Start fresh when the session's value lies in what it concluded. Write a brief that extracts the decisions, the constraints, and the rationale, then launch a new session with that brief. The new session starts with signal and skips the noise.

A brief extracts decisions from the old session, starts a new session with clean context, and executes without stale noise

The brief-first pattern keeps session length bounded, reduces cache read costs, and surfaces the conclusions that matter. This post shows when to resume, when to start fresh, how to extract a brief, and the cost implications of session growth.

Key Takeaways

  • Resume restores the full conversation, including stale context and dead-end exploration that inflates cache read costs.
  • Session state (unfinished goals, pending approvals, permission modes) requires resume; session conclusions (decisions, constraints, rationale) do not.
  • A brief extracts the conclusions from a long session and starts a new session with clean context, reducing noise and cost.
  • Cache reads account for the majority of agentic work costs; every turn added to a session increases what future turns re-read.
  • Session retention defaults to 30 days; transcripts older than cleanupPeriodDays are removed and cannot be resumed.

Understanding Claude Code Session Architecture

Claude Code stores sessions as JSONL transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/ (or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/projects/ when set). Each project directory holds one conversation per session ID. When you resume, Claude Code reads the entire transcript into the prompt and continues from the last message. The session lookup order searches the current project directory first, then other projects on the same machine, and finally falls back to a cross-directory ID match.

Claude Code locates the session file, reads the full transcript, and continues with the loaded context

A session that ended with error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd can be resumed with higher limits, but the agent re-reads the entire history that led to the limit in the first place. The automatic session management APIs (ClaudeSDKClient in Python, continue: true in TypeScript) track the most recent session in the directory and resume it without manual ID handling. That convenience makes the resume-by-default trap easier to fall into.

Sessions survive machine sleep but not shutdown. A session interrupted by shutdown shows as failed if less than 48 hours have passed, or stopped if more. Attaching or replying to a stopped session resumes its saved conversation, provided transcript cleanup has not removed it. The default retention is 30 days. Past that point, the session row remains in agent view but the transcript is gone.

Claude Code session architecture

When Resume Makes Sense: State vs Conclusions

Resume when the session holds state you cannot easily rebuild. The state is the point. Start fresh when the session's value lies in what it concluded. The table shows the split:

Situation Action Reason
Goal still in progress Resume The unfinished work is the state you need
Plan awaiting approval Resume The plan itself is the pending state
Background work didn't finish Resume The partial progress is not easily restated
Permission mode set deliberately Resume The mode is part of the session's setup
Session concluded with a decision Start fresh with brief The decision is a conclusion, not state
Exploratory work led to a constraint Start fresh with brief The constraint is a conclusion, not state
Session hit max turns on a refactor Start fresh with brief The transcript is now noise
Session ran for hours across topics Start fresh with brief The early turns are stale

A decision point checks whether the session holds state or conclusions, then resumes or starts fresh accordingly

The state includes goals Claude is actively pursuing, plans awaiting your approval, permission modes you configured, and partial work that cannot be summarized. The conclusions include decisions Claude reached, constraints it discovered, and rationale it explained. Conclusions compress into a brief. State does not.

A session that ended with error_max_turns after a large refactor holds conclusions, not state. The refactor either succeeded or it didn't. The decisions that worked compress into a brief. Resuming re-reads the 300 turns that led to the limit, most of which were file reads and tool calls exploring options that didn't pan out. A new session with a brief starts with the decisions and skips the exploration.

The Brief-First Pattern: Replacing Long Sessions

A brief extracts what a session concluded and feeds that into a new session. The brief is a markdown file or a prompt. It holds the decisions, the constraints, and the rationale. The new session starts with that context and none of the stale tool output from the old session.

The pattern has three steps:

  1. Run the exploratory session to completion or until it reaches a natural pause
  2. Extract a brief of the conclusions (manually or by asking Claude to summarize)
  3. Start a new session with the brief as the initial prompt

The TypeScript example shows the pattern in SDK code. The first session runs a refactor and captures the session ID. The second session extracts a brief by resuming with a summary request. The third session starts fresh with that brief:

import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

// Step 1: Run the exploratory session
let exploratoryId: string | undefined;
for await (const message of query({
  prompt: "Refactor the auth module to use the new token format",
  options: { allowedTools: ["Read", "Edit", "Grep", "Glob"] }
})) {
  if (message.type === "result") {
    exploratoryId = message.session_id;
    if (message.subtype === "success") {
      console.log("Refactor complete:", message.result);
    }
  }
}

// Step 2: Extract a brief
let brief = "";
if (exploratoryId) {
  for await (const message of query({
    prompt: "Summarize the decisions we made, the constraints we found, and why each change was necessary. Write it as a brief I can paste into a new session.",
    options: { resume: exploratoryId, allowedTools: [] }
  })) {
    if (message.type === "result" && message.subtype === "success") {
      brief = message.result;
    }
  }
}

// Step 3: Start fresh with the brief
for await (const message of query({
  prompt: `${brief}\n\nNow implement the remaining endpoints using these decisions.`,
  options: { allowedTools: ["Read", "Edit", "Write", "Grep", "Glob"] }
})) {
  if (message.type === "result" && message.subtype === "success") {
    console.log("Implementation complete:", message.result);
  }
}

The brief holds the signal. The exploratory session's transcript held the signal plus 200 turns of noise. The new session starts with the signal and builds from there. The cache read cost on each turn is proportional to the brief's size, not the exploratory session's size.

An exploratory session runs to completion, extracts a brief of conclusions, and starts a new session with the brief as context

The brief can be a file you write by hand after reviewing the session, or a file Claude generates when you ask it to summarize. The manual version takes more time but produces a denser brief. The generated version is faster but sometimes includes unnecessary detail. Both work. The key is that the new session starts with conclusions, not history.

Session Management Strategies in Practice

The automatic session management APIs resume the most recent session in the directory by default. The TypeScript continue: true option and the Python continue_conversation=True option both behave this way. That default makes sense for a chat interface where every prompt is a continuation of the last. It makes less sense for agentic work where each session solves a distinct problem.

The Python example shows the difference between automatic continuation and manual session control:

// Automatic continuation: good for chat, risky for tasks
import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

for await (const message of query({
  prompt: "Fix the validation bug in auth.ts",
  options: { continue: true, allowedTools: ["Read", "Edit"] }
})) {
  if (message.type === "result" && message.subtype === "success") {
    console.log(message.result);
  }
}

// This continues the most recent session, which might be
// a three-hour refactor from yesterday. The bug fix inherits
// that session's stale context.

// Manual session control: start fresh per task
for await (const message of query({
  prompt: "Fix the validation bug in auth.ts",
  options: { allowedTools: ["Read", "Edit"] }
})) {
  if (message.type === "result" && message.subtype === "success") {
    console.log(message.result);
  }
}

// This starts a new session. The bug fix gets clean context.

The manual approach starts a new session for each task unless you explicitly pass a resume ID. That makes session growth an intentional choice rather than a default. The automatic approach treats every prompt as a follow-up unless you explicitly start fresh. The manual approach is safer for production workflows where tasks are independent.

The fork option creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original's history. The original stays unchanged. Use fork to try a different direction while keeping the option to go back. Fork is not a substitute for the brief-first pattern. A forked session inherits the same stale context as a resumed session. The fork simply preserves the original session so you can return to it later.

Session management strategies

Cost Implications: Cache Reads and Context Growth

Anthropic's Opus 5.5 announcement states that cache reads account for the majority of agentic and coding work costs. Every turn you add to a session becomes part of what later turns re-read. The cache read cost is proportional to the session's total token count, not the new prompt's token count. A 500-token prompt sent to a 50,000-token session re-reads 50,000 cached tokens and adds 500 new tokens. The cache read cost dominates.

Each turn re-reads the full session, so cost grows with session size, not prompt size

The table compares the cache read cost of a 10-turn session, a 100-turn session, and a fresh session:

Session size Avg tokens per turn Total session tokens Cache reads per new turn New prompt tokens Total cost per turn
10 turns 2,000 20,000 20,000 500 20,500 tokens
100 turns 2,000 200,000 200,000 500 200,500 tokens
Fresh 0 0 0 500 500 tokens

The 100-turn session re-reads 400 times more tokens than the new prompt contains. The fresh session reads only the new prompt. The brief-first pattern keeps the session size bounded by extracting the conclusions and starting fresh before the session grows to 100 turns. A brief that compresses 100 turns of exploration into 2,000 tokens reduces the cache read cost by 99%.

The idle compaction feature compacts long conversations while the terminal session is idle, shortly before a one-hour prompt cache expires. Compaction is unavailable when feature-flag fetching is disabled, which includes sessions on third-party providers and sessions with DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC set. Even when available, compaction addresses cache expiry, not session bloat. A session that grew to 300 turns over three hours exceeds the cache window regardless of compaction.

Session Retention, Naming, and Deletion Workflow

Claude Code removes transcripts older than cleanupPeriodDays, which defaults to 30. A session removed by cleanup shows in agent view but cannot be resumed. The row says "This session's saved conversation is no longer on disk" when you try to open it. claude rm <id> deletes the row unless the session is running or its transcript still exists.

A session remains until it exceeds the cleanup period, then the transcript is removed and resume fails

The --name flag sets the session's display name in agent view when launching with --bg. The name appears in claude agents output and makes it easier to identify sessions later. The flag works only at launch. You cannot rename a session after it starts.

The backgrounded session dispatch workflow shows how --name combines with --bg:

// Launch a named background session
$ claude --bg --name "auth-refactor" "Refactor auth module to new format"

// Output:
// backgrounded · 7c5dcf5d · auth-refactor
// claude agents list sessions
// claude attach 7c5dcf5d open in this terminal
// claude logs 7c5dcf5d show recent output
// claude stop 7c5dcf5d stop this session

The session ID 7c5dcf5d is the short form. The full ID is a UUID. Both work with --resume. The name auth-refactor appears in agent view and makes the session easier to find when you have multiple sessions running. The name does not affect session lookup. --resume requires the ID, not the name.

The session stop and resume behavior differs depending on how long ago the session last made progress. A session that was waiting on input stays under "Needs input" after a machine restart. A session that was running shows as failed within 48 hours or stopped past 48 hours. Attaching or replying resumes the saved conversation, provided cleanup has not removed it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does resuming a session cost more than starting fresh?

Yes. Resume re-reads the entire transcript on every turn, which shows up as cache read tokens. A 100-turn session re-reads 100 turns of context. A fresh session reads only the new prompt. The cache read cost is proportional to session size, not prompt size.

When should I use --fork instead of --resume?

Use fork when you want to try a different direction while preserving the original session. Fork creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original's history. The original stays unchanged. Fork is not a substitute for starting fresh. A forked session inherits the same stale context as a resumed session.

Can I resume a session from a different machine?

No, unless you mirror transcripts to shared storage with a SessionStore adapter. By default, sessions are stored locally under ~/.claude/projects/ and are only accessible from the same machine.

How long are sessions retained before cleanup?

Sessions are retained for cleanupPeriodDays, which defaults to 30 days. After that period, the transcript is removed and the session cannot be resumed. The session row remains in agent view but shows "This session's saved conversation is no longer on disk" when you try to open it.

What happens if I resume a session whose agent no longer exists?

The session continues with the default tools and its transcript opens with a warning naming the agent. Claude Code searches the session's own directory for the agent first, so a project-scoped agent still loads when the session is resumed from another directory, provided you've trusted that workspace.

Conclusion: Building a Sustainable Session Strategy

The brief-first pattern treats session length as a cost to manage, not an asset to preserve. Resume when the session holds unfinished work you cannot rebuild. Start fresh when the session's value lies in what it concluded. Write a brief that extracts the decisions, the constraints, and the rationale, then launch a new session with that brief. The new session starts with signal and skips the noise. Session growth is now an intentional choice tied to unfinished state, not a reflexive default.

articles.title: Remotion vs. CoAnimator When Your Product Demo Needs an Update
articles.description: You publish a product demo on Friday. On Monday, the Save button moves into an overflow menu.  You...
articles.body_html:
You publish a product demo on Friday. On Monday, the Save button moves into an overflow menu.

You replace the recording. Now the caption appears before the click, the voiceover describes the old UI, and the next scene starts too soon. Someone has to fix all three before the video can go live again.

That’s the edit I’d use to compare Remotion and CoAnimator. Both can work with coding agents. What matters after launch is whether the person who owns the video can make the change, review it, and verify the new export.

What you edit in each tool

Remotion uses React components and props

In Remotion, the composition defines how the video looks and changes over time. Props can hold details that vary between exports, such as a release title, screenshot, or translated caption. If you expose those details as inputs, the next release can reuse the composition without a code change. Remotion’s guide to parameterized videos

The Remotion team’s Agent Skills demo shows one example of a video made with this workflow.

CoAnimator uses editable scenes and a visual timeline

CoAnimator gives you a desktop editor with a stage and timeline. You can ask a coding agent to revise a scene, then inspect the footage, captions, and timing in the editor. That’s useful when the person approving the edit needs to see exactly where it lands in the video. CoAnimator documentation

This showcase gives you a view of the editor around the animation. Use the revision tests below to judge how it fits your own project.

A small Remotion composition you can render

In an existing Remotion starter project, save this as src/release-title.tsx. It registers its own composition and can be passed directly to the render command.

import {
  AbsoluteFill,
  Composition,
  interpolate,
  registerRoot,
  useCurrentFrame,
  useVideoConfig,
} from 'remotion';

type ReleaseTitleProps = {title: string};

function ReleaseTitle({title}: ReleaseTitleProps) {
  const frame = useCurrentFrame();
  const {fps} = useVideoConfig();

  const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, fps], [0, 1], {
    extrapolateRight: 'clamp',
  });

  return (
    <AbsoluteFill
      style={{
        alignItems: 'center',
        justifyContent: 'center',
        padding: 96,
        backgroundColor: '#ffffff',
        color: '#172554',
        fontSize: 80,
        textAlign: 'center',
        opacity,
      }}
    >
      {title}
    </AbsoluteFill>
  );
}

function Root() {
  return (
    <Composition
      id="ReleaseTitle"
      component={ReleaseTitle}
      durationInFrames={90}
      fps={30}
      width={1920}
      height={1080}
      defaultProps={{title: 'Version 2.4 is live'}}
    />
  );
}

registerRoot(Root);

Render the default title, then pass in a new title and render again:

npx remotion render src/release-title.tsx ReleaseTitle out/v24.mp4

npx remotion render src/release-title.tsx ReleaseTitle out/v25.mp4 \
  --props='{"title":"Version 2.5 adds saved filters and shared views"}'

Watch both exports. The title changes and the fade stays the same. This is the smallest version of a changelog workflow where release data changes more often than the layout. Remotion render command

Three edits to run in both tools

Build the same short demo in each tool using the same recording, captions, and closing card. Save a baseline export before making changes. Then run these edits separately so you can tell where the work accumulates.

1. Change the title and screenshot

In Remotion, expose the title and screenshot as props and rerender with new inputs. In CoAnimator, open the matching scene in the timeline and update the title and image, or ask the agent to make those two changes.

Use a long title and a screenshot with a different aspect ratio. Check both MP4s for text overflow and poor cropping. If a routine copy change needs a manual layout adjustment, count that time.

2. Replace footage after the interface changes

In Remotion, replace the clip in the composition and update the cue frames for the caption and callout. In CoAnimator, swap the clip in the timeline and move those cues, or give the agent a request with a clear boundary:

Replace the recording in scene 2 with overflow-menu.mp4.
Show the menu opening before highlighting Save.
Move the caption to match the click.
Keep the intro and closing card unchanged.

Use the same replacement clip in both tools. Replay a few seconds on either side of the edit and check the narration, caption timing, and transition. If you use Git, the diff can show which files changed. Playback tells you whether those changes work together.

3. Update a closing card across 20 videos

In Remotion, put the card in a shared component and feed its URL from a common setting. Update that setting and rerender each video with its own inputs.

In CoAnimator, check whether your projects reference a shared card or contain separate copies. Apply the change to the shared source or update the copies, then export through the app or CLI.

Record how many files needed edits and how many exports you had to check. A scripted render helps with the export step. Whether the URL change takes one edit or twenty depends on how the projects share that card.

Rendering and licensing

Remotion CoAnimator
Render options Local CLI, server-side rendering, or AWS Lambda Local app and scripted exports through coa
Free option Eligible individuals and organizations with up to three people 720p local exports with a watermark
Paid option Creators at $25 per seat per month, or Automators at $0.01 per render with a $100 monthly minimum One-time license listed at $299 as a limited-time offer, with watermark-free exports up to 4K

Compare the license and the cost of running the workflow. Cloud compute and storage can add to a Remotion bill. With CoAnimator, include the machines you use to render and any external agent or media services. Remotion pricing · CoAnimator pricing

The handoff test I’d use to decide

Give the project and the replacement footage to the person who will maintain the demo. Ask them to make the revision and verify the new MP4 on a second machine. Record the time from receiving the footage to approving the export, including any missing assets, setup work, or requests for help.

I’d start with Remotion if most revisions are changes to data in a stable layout. I’d try CoAnimator if most revisions involve footage and timing that someone needs to review in a visual timeline. A team producing both automated changelogs and individually edited demos may use a different workflow for each.

FAQ

Can CoAnimator replace Remotion?

It can cover demos, tutorials, and launch videos that someone edits as individual projects. If your app builds many videos from customer data, Remotion’s props and rendering APIs give you a direct way to implement that workflow.

Can I use Remotion commercially on the free license?

Yes, if you meet the eligibility terms for individuals or organizations with up to three people. Remotion license and pricing

Can both tools render from a script?

Yes. Remotion offers a CLI and Node.js APIs. CoAnimator offers the coa CLI. Run a test export on the machine that will render your real projects, using the same fonts, footage, and output settings.

Which part takes your team longer after a release: making the edit or verifying the new export?

articles.title: I Don't Need Your Permission
articles.description: Software engineers have got it tough right now. I look at senior jobs asking for more years of...
articles.body_html:
Software engineers have got it tough right now. I look at senior jobs asking for more years of experience than I’ve even been in software. Then I look at the entry-level work I’m seeing and it’s like, So you want me to teach AI how to do the job I’ve been trying to get?

Yeah. That sucks.

And when somebody says they’re afraid AI is going to take away their livelihood, I get it. That fear is 100% understandable. I’ve spent years learning to design and build software, and now part of the work available to me is teaching the very thing that could replace me how to do it.

Then I go to a dev site, click “Top,” and I swear eight out of ten articles are about AI. I go to another one. Same thing. Every. Single. One. Of. Them. It’s the nature of the beast right now.

So what am I going to do? Take a system I designed, teach AI how I want it built, and check whether it can follow that design consistently. I can use the same tools reshaping my job to better my own situation, and I get to make choices about how I use them. If my own hardware can handle the work, I’ll run it locally. If I need more compute than I have, I’ll decide whether that particular job is worth sending to the cloud.

Am I happy that the job market looks like this? No. Am I going to sit here and wait for it to look the way I wanted it to? No, no, no, baby girl.

When I ask, “Why can’t you adapt?” I’m asking myself that, too. And some days my answer is, “I’d really rather just have a job.”

Here’s where I get a little philosophical about it. XD

I am more than software. I am more than the cloud. I am more than my job.

I write songs. I make games. I have stories I want to tell. I still have to figure out how to pay my bills. I just don’t need the answer to that question to tell me who I am. I create stuff, and I’m figuring out how to make a living doing it.

I’ve had music on SoundCloud that was used to train AI. I haven’t heard it play one of my songs back note for note. I get why another musician might feel differently about their work being used. For me, it’s wild how fast it can pick up patterns that took me years to learn. I still think I can outperform it in creativity. Output per second? Yeah, it’s got me there. XD

And that speed changes who gets to make things. I can write a story, design a game around it, and build it. I can’t afford a whole team of modelers, texture artists, and animators. When I can, I want to hire artists. Today, if I can use AI to get a character into a build and hand the game to a friend to see if it’s fun, I don’t see anything unethical about doing that.

That’s what I mean when I say AI is turning things from service to creation. I could be the guy who loses a gig because a developer can generate a music track now. I could also be the guy who finally gets his game playable because he can make an asset he couldn’t afford to commission. Both of those guys are me. Of course people who make a living doing this work are worried. And of course the person who’s had a game idea for ten years is excited that they can finally try it.

Would I prefer AI to be more tame and regulated? Absolutely. Sometimes it feels like we bought a pressure washer and decided to do the dishes with it. And this is already bigger than artists and software engineers. The tech is out there at massive scale. We’re going to put it in a bunch of places, find out where it actually helps, and probably spend a few years wishing we’d left some things alone.

Kind of like smartphones. We put everything on them, and now some days I miss snapping a flip phone shut and being done.

Hello, T9.

Anyway, this was a real roundabout way to give myself permission to create. I could’ve been working on my game this whole time. XD

articles.title: Fix 'sorry, too many clients already' and hanging queries in Node pg
articles.description: A leaked pg pool client makes request 11 wait forever, and 10 default pools hit max_connections. Measured on pg 8.23.1, Postgres 17.12.
articles.body_html:
Ten requests leaked a connection in my Node service, and request number 11 never got an answer. No error, no log line, no timeout. I reproduced it with pg 8.23.1, Node 24.22.1 and PostgreSQL 17.12: after 8 seconds the query was still waiting, and I could have waited all day. The second failure, sorry, too many clients already, took 12 app instances with the default pool to trigger. Both are one-line fixes once you know what to look at.

Failure 1: the query that waits forever

pg.Pool defaults to max: 10 and connectionTimeoutMillis: 0. Zero means "wait without limit". So if ten checked-out clients never come back, the eleventh caller sits in a queue and nothing tells you.

Here is the handler pattern I had. It throws between connect() and release():

async function handler() {
  const c = await pool.connect();
  await c.query('select 1');
  throw new Error('boom'); // release() never runs
}

I ran it 10 times, then asked for one more connection. Results, one process per setup:

setup request 11
leak, default pool no answer after 8000 ms, pool.waitingCount = 1
leak, connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000 timeout exceeded when trying to connect after 2000 ms
try/finally with release() ok in 0 to 1 ms, pool total stays at 1

The timeout does not fix the leak. It turns a silent hang into an error you can see, alert on and trace to the handler. The finally is the actual fix:

const { Pool } = require('pg');

const pool = new Pool({
  max: 10,
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000, // fail loudly instead of queueing forever
});

async function handler() {
  const c = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await c.query('select 1');
    // ...your work
  } finally {
    c.release(); // runs on return and on throw
  }
}

If you can, use pool.query() for single statements. It checks the client out and releases it for you, so there is nothing to forget.

Failure 2: sorry, too many clients already

Postgres defaults to max_connections = 100, and 3 of those are reserved for superusers (superuser_reserved_connections). Your app role gets 97. Each Node process has its own pool, so the math is instances x pool max, not pool max.

I started N processes, each with a pool of max and each opening all of its connections at once, using a normal non-superuser role:

instances x pool max wanted connected failed error
5 x 10 50 50 0 none
10 x 10 100 97 3 remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute
12 x 10 120 97 23 the same message, plus sorry, too many clients already
10 x 9 90 90 0 none

Two things surprised me. First, 10 instances of a default pool already break, because of the 3 reserved slots. Second, the first error message you see is not "too many clients". It is the "reserved for SUPERUSER" one, and it sends people looking at their role instead of their pool size.

A caveat on my own run: I first connected as postgres (a superuser) and got 100 of 100 connections. Superusers can use the reserved slots. If you test pool limits as your admin user, you will think everything is fine.

The sizing rule I use now 

pool max  =  floor((max_connections - 3 - headroom) / instances)

Headroom is for migrations, psql sessions and a deploy where old and new instances overlap. With max_connections = 100, 10 instances and 10 spare slots, that is floor(87 / 10) = 8 per instance. Rolling deploys count too: if you run 10 and start 10 more before the old ones stop, size for 20.

If you cannot shrink the pool enough, put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front. I did not test it here, so treat that as a pointer and not a result.

See it before it hurts

Log the pool counters on an interval, and ask Postgres who is holding the slots:

setInterval(() => {
  console.log({ total: pool.totalCount, idle: pool.idleCount, waiting: pool.waitingCount });
}, 10_000).unref();

select usename, state, count(*) from pg_stat_activity group by 1, 2 order by 3 desc;

A leak looks like idle: 0 with total stuck at your max while traffic is low. Many idle in transaction rows point at a handler that opened a transaction and never finished it.

Checklist

  1. Set connectionTimeoutMillis on every pool. Zero is never what you want in production.
  2. Every manual pool.connect() needs a try/finally with release(). Search your code for .connect() and read each one.
  3. Watch pool.totalCount, pool.idleCount and pool.waitingCount. A waitingCount above zero for more than a moment is your early warning.
  4. Do the instances x max math against show max_connections on the real server, and leave headroom.
  5. Test as the app role, not as a superuser.

What I did not test

One pg version (8.23.1), one Node version (24.22.1), one Postgres build (17.12, the embedded-postgres binary, not a managed service). Managed Postgres often has a different max_connections tied to instance size, so read yours. I did not test ORMs or pool wrappers that set their own timeouts, and I did not test PgBouncer. The lab scripts are small enough to copy: one file for the leak, one worker for the instance math.

When your Node service runs out of Postgres connections, what is it that you find first: a hang, a timeout, or the "too many clients" error?

articles.title: Building Clockwork: An AI-Native 2D Game Engine Verified End-to-End with Kane CLI
articles.description: Making a small 2D game usually means juggling several tools. You lay out the level in one place, tune...
articles.body_html:
Making a small 2D game usually means juggling several tools. You lay out the level in one place, tune physics and behaviors in code, build the HUD somewhere else, and playtest by hand. Each hand-off loses context, and "does it still work?" gets answered by clicking around.

Clockwork is a 2D game engine that runs in the browser and keeps all of that in one app. You build scenes, attach behaviors, write rules, design the HUD, play the game, and share it from the same window. Kane CLI then drives that same app in a real Chrome browser to prove the editor and the games work end to end.

We built Clockwork during the KaneCLI Online Hackathon. This post covers the engine itself and how Kane CLI tests it. A companion post covers the built-in AI agent and how it uses Kane to verify the games it builds.

Inside the engine

Scenes, layers and parallax

A Clockwork project holds one or more scenes. Each scene has a world size, a background and an ordered stack of layers. Every layer has its own opacity and its own parallax factors on X and Y, so a distant sky can scroll slower than the ground the player runs on.

Clockwork Meadows, the showcase starter, uses four layers: Sky, Mountains, Forest, and Meadow and actors. Its world is 18,400 × 1,200 pixels and holds 227 objects. Camera follow keeps the player in view across that width. Fixed-screen games shrink to fit instead, so the whole playfield stays visible in a smaller window.

Behaviors

Clockwork ships 27 composable behaviors, defined in src/engine/model/behavior-catalog.ts. You attach them to objects in the Inspector and tune their parameters, and every parameter shows its default with a Reset button. They include:

  • Movement: platformer-controller, top-down-controller, rotate-thrust, flap, mover, snake.
  • Enemies: patrol, follow, formation, stompable, melee.
  • Game objects: collectible, hazard, checkpoint, exit-gate, spawner.
  • Combat: health, shooter, projectile.
  • Arcade: ball, paddle, ai-paddle.
  • Timing and camera: timer, countdown, camera-follow.

A behavior is a small, focused unit. The Meadows player, Marlow, combines a platformer controller (speed 340 px/s, a 135 ms jump buffer, a tuned jump cut) with camera follow. A coin is just an object with collectible. You build new mechanics by combining behaviors.

Rules, variables and HUD widgets

Behaviors cover moment-to-moment play. Rules cover game logic. A rule pairs a list of conditions (overlap, input, timer, scene start, variable) with a list of actions (set, add to or toggle a variable, spawn a prefab, destroy, play a sound, show a message, change scene). That's enough to say "when the player overlaps a coin, add 1 to score and destroy the coin" without code. Variables hold game state such as score, lives or shards, and HUD widgets bind to them so the screen always shows the live value. Rules and variables live in the editor's Logic tab. Look, animation, audio and UI live in Presentation.

Prefabs, undo and redo

Prefabs let you define an object once and stamp out copies. Every edit goes through one command registry. The editor footer states the contract: "One completed gesture = one revision and one undo entry." Dragging an object, changing a field or applying a batch of changes therefore always undoes as a single step.

Starters

You can start a project from Blank, from one of three classic templates (Platformer, Top-down, Puzzle), from a written brief, or from one of 14 genre starters:

Space Shooter, Space Invaders, Asteroid Field, Ping Pong, Brick Breaker, Flappy Flyer, Platform Jumper, Clockwork Meadows, Meadow Sandbox, Endless Runner, Arena Survival, Falling Objects, Maze Escape and Snake.

Each starter is built from the same behaviors, rules and HUD widgets you use in your own projects, so you can open any of them and change how it works.

Clockwork Meadows is the largest. You run the meadow, stomp dragons, light checkpoints, collect sun shards and reach the summit camp. Press Play and the four layers scroll at their own rates behind the player.

Share and ship

When a game is ready, the Ship panel publishes it:

  • Share links. Clockwork freezes the current project into a read-only snapshot served at /s/:snapshotId (src/routes.tsx). Anyone with the link plays that exact version, and later edits in the editor don't change it. You choose how long the link lives.
  • Zip export. Clockwork packages the game and its assets as a standalone static build (src/engine/io/build.ts) that you can host on any static web server.
  • Project file. The whole project also exports as .clockwork.json, which the New Project dialog can import.

Snapshots also matter for testing. AI Play and the agent's Kane checks run against a snapshot rather than the live editor, so the version under test can't change mid-run.

Kane CLI tests the engine end to end

Unit tests cover the engine's logic: pnpm test runs 176 tests across 27 files, and all 176 pass. Unit tests can't show that a person can open the app, build a game and play it. Kane CLI covers that.

Clockwork keeps a saved Kane test at .testmuai/tests/engine-template-e2e_test.md. It is a plain Markdown file with a short front-matter block (mode: testing, max_steps: 50, timeout: 480, target: chrome) and one step written in plain English. In that step Kane:

  1. Opens Clockwork and creates a project named "Engine E2E Platformer" from the Platform Jumper starter.
  2. Checks that the scene canvas and the Scene hierarchy are visible.
  3. Selects the "Jumper" row in the hierarchy and records its Object Y in the Inspector.
  4. Presses ArrowUp twice to nudge the object, then Control+Z twice, and checks that Object Y is back to the recorded value.
  5. Presses Play and checks for the game canvas and the CORES and LIVES HUD labels, with LIVES reading 3.
  6. Presses Space and checks that LIVES still reads 3.
  7. Presses R to restart and checks the HUD again, with LIVES at 3.
  8. Returns to the editor and checks that the project is still open with its canvas and hierarchy.

One flow covers project creation, the hierarchy, the Inspector, keyboard editing, undo, Play, the HUD, restart and the return to the editor.

Run it with one command:

pnpm kane:engine-e2e

scripts/kane/engine-e2e.mjs runs the saved test through kane-cli testmd run. It prints one compact JSON result and keeps the raw NDJSON stream, a result summary and the evidence pack under .testmuai/.

The first authored run passed in 286 s. A later run of the one-command variant, pnpm kane:engine-e2e:dev, started the app from cold, replayed the saved step and passed in 89 s. For this post we ran pnpm kane:engine-e2e again. It passed 1 of 1 steps, replayed, in 134 s (session c6bc88c1).

Because the test is a Markdown file in the repo, it is versioned with the code, can be reviewed in a pull request, and runs again with the same command.

Layout precision: Clockwork's HUD audit

Kane reads Clockwork's HUDs as page text and clicks their buttons, so those panels have to stay clear of each other. Clockwork has its own layout audit for this, separate from Kane: pnpm test:hud (scripts/kane/hud-overlap-check.mts).

The audit connects to Chrome over the DevTools protocol. It builds every template and starter, publishes each one as a snapshot, and opens it in three player modes: real-time play, manual Test Mode, and Test Mode with planned check steps. It opens each mode at two viewport sizes, 1280×800 and 1024×640. On every page it checks two things:

  1. Every button and input can be clicked. It hit-tests each control at its centre and at four inset points, and the element under each point must be the control itself.
  2. No two HUD panels overlap. This covers the AI and Test Mode readouts, control groups, the game's own HUD widgets, the "Made with Clockwork" badge and the PAUSED/Restart pill.

Our run printed:

108/108 layouts clean.

That is 18 starting points × 3 modes × 2 viewports. The audit also writes a full report to .data/hud-overlap/report.json.

Wrap-up

Clockwork puts a 2D game engine, its editor and its verification in one browser app. Its runtime, physics, 27 behaviors, rules, HUD widgets and Test Mode are built for that workflow. Kane CLI proves the main editor path in a real browser with a saved test you can rerun anytime. The companion post shows how Clockwork's built-in agent uses Kane to check the games it builds.

  • Source code: https://github.com/tope-olajide/clockwork
  • Demo video: https://youtu.be/ybe9e93r4SU

articles.body_html:
RepoDNA v1.5.4 Released: Browser Storage Reliability and Safer Analysis Restoration

I'm pleased to announce the stable release of RepoDNA v1.5.4, published on November 26, 2026.

RepoDNA is an open-source, local-first repository intelligence platform designed to help developers understand software projects through architecture analysis, dependency visualization, code metrics and Git history.

This maintenance release concentrates on storage consistency, analysis recovery and release integrity.

Why this release matters
