3:04 AM

I woke up at 3:04 and knew, with the kind of certainty you only get at 3:04, that the deploy was broken.

Not a feeling. A fact. I had shipped it at 4:47 yesterday afternoon, late, because the afternoon had gone sideways and the fix had taken three tries, and I had watched the checks go green and told myself green meant done. Now it was 3:04 and I knew green had meant nothing. Somewhere a user was staring at a blank page, or a form that ate their input, or a button that did nothing when clicked. I could see the message I would have to send in the morning. I could see the exact words. I reached for my phone.

3:04 AM, draft 1, deleted

Hi, sorry to message early. I think yesterday's deploy might have broken something. I'm checking now. Will update soon.

Too vague. "Might have broken something" is what you write when you want credit for honesty without admitting anything. And "will update soon" is a promise I could not keep at 3:04 in the morning, in the dark, with my eyes still half closed. I deleted it and opened the dashboard instead.

Green. Everything green. Uptime green, error rate flat, response times normal. I refreshed it. Still green. I refreshed it again, slower this time, like the numbers might change their mind if I gave them a second to think about it.

They did not change their mind. Nothing was broken. I knew that, and I was still awake.

3:11 AM, draft 2, deleted

Quick heads up, I woke up worried about the deploy. Dashboard looks fine but I wanted to check if anyone has seen anything odd.

No. "I woke up worried" is not a sentence you send to people you work with. It is a sentence you send to a friend at 3:11 in the morning, and even then you think twice. And "has anyone seen anything odd" would start a thread at 3:11 in the morning, and the thread would still be there at 9:00, and someone would reply "what kind of odd?" and I would have to answer "I don't know, just odd," and that is how you become the person who cries wolf about a deploy that was fine.

I put the phone down. I stared at the ceiling. The ceiling had nothing to say.

The thing about 3:04 is that the worry picks a shape and wears it. Yesterday the shape was the deploy. Last week it was an email I sent with the wrong attachment. The week before that it was a meeting where I said "sounds good" to something I had not actually understood, and spent the whole night waiting for someone to find out. The shape changes. The hour does not.

3:26 AM, draft 3, deleted

Hey, sorry, couldn't sleep. Just wanted to double check the deploy from yesterday. All good on my end, dashboard is green. Ignore this, I'll check properly in the morning.

"Ignore this" in a message nobody can ignore. If I sent that, someone would read it at 7:30 over breakfast and spend their whole morning wondering what I had seen that they had not. I deleted it before I could talk myself into sending it as a joke. It was not a joke. It was the truth wearing a joke's clothes, and I have learned to spot that trick by now, because I have used it on myself at least a dozen times.

I got up. I made tea. I stood in the kitchen in the dark, because turning the light on felt like admitting I was properly awake, and I was not ready to admit that. The tea was too hot. I held it anyway. Holding something hot is a good way to be awake without having to do anything about being awake.

While the tea cooled, I opened the deploy diff on my phone. I read it line by line, in the dark, squinting. Forty-one lines changed. I remembered writing every one of them. I remembered the third try, the one that worked, and the two tries before it, and the exact moment I realised the second try had been fixing the wrong thing. The diff was fine. The diff had been fine at 4:47. The tests had passed at 4:47. Nothing about 3:04 had changed the diff. The only thing 3:04 had changed was me.

3:52 AM, draft 4, deleted

Morning all, just flagging that I shipped the fix late yesterday. It passed all checks but I want to re-verify the edge cases first thing. If anything looks off, ping me.

That one was almost sendable. It sounded responsible. It sounded like a person who had their act together. The problem was that it was 3:52 in the morning and the person writing it did not have their act together, and sending a responsible-sounding message at 3:52 is just a worried message with better manners. Also, "re-verify the edge cases first thing" meant I had already decided to spend my morning re-checking work that was already checked, because the checking was the only thing that made the worrying stop for a while. I have done that before. It works for about an hour. Then something else needs checking.

I went back to bed. I lay there and tried the thing where you count backwards from a hundred. I got to eighty-six and started thinking about a question I had been sitting on for a month. Not a work question, not exactly. A question about what I was doing, and whether the shape of it was right, and whether I was building the thing I meant to build or just getting very good at the small part of it. The kind of question that does not fit in a standup. The kind of question you do not ask at 3:52 in the morning because you know the answer will be whatever the dark says, and the dark always says the worst version.

4:37 AM, draft 5, deleted

I know this is random but I've been thinking about the way we do deploys late in the day and whether we should stop doing that. The fix yesterday was fine but the timing wasn't great. Can we talk about it?

That was closer to the real thing, and that was why I deleted it fastest. A message sent at 4:37 in the morning about deploy timing is not about deploy timing. It is about a person who is awake at 4:37 in the morning and wants someone to know. The deploy timing question was real, and it deserved a real conversation, in daylight, when I could say it properly. But I did not want a conversation about deploy timing. I wanted someone to tell me the worry was normal, and that is not a message. That is a conversation you have with a person, sitting down, not a text you fire off before dawn.

I fell asleep somewhere after five. I do not remember falling asleep. I remember the light changing, the grey coming in under the curtains, and then my alarm going off at 7:30, and the strange, ordinary feeling of having survived another night of nothing happening.

Morning. I checked the dashboard again, in daylight, like a normal person. Green. I checked the messages. Nothing from anyone. Nobody had noticed anything, because there was nothing to notice. The deploy had been fine all along. The deploy had never been the problem.

I opened the chat. I typed a message. Not an apology. Not a heads-up. Not a flag.

7:42 AM, sent

Hey, can I ask you something? Not urgent, just been thinking about it for a while. Do you ever feel like we're getting really good at shipping and I still don't know if we're shipping the right thing? Can we talk about it this week, properly, not in a standup?

I stared at it for a long time before I sent it. Then I sent it, and I put the phone down, and I went and made breakfast, and the reply came while the toast was browning.

Yeah. Friday? Coffee's on me.

Friday. Good. I had three days to figure out how to say the rest of it. The dashboard stayed green all morning. The deploy stayed fine. And somewhere between the toast and the reply, I understood something I had missed all night: the worry at 3:04 had never been about whether the code worked. It was about whether I was allowed to ask the question underneath it. I had spent the whole night drafting messages about a deploy that was fine, because a deploy is a safe thing to worry about. The question was not safe. The question was the thing.

I still wake up at 3:04 sometimes. The shape changes. Last Tuesday it was an email again. But now, when it happens, I know what to look for: the thing underneath the thing. The message I keep deleting is never the message I need to send.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: The Third Cup: You Don't Have to Run Faster Than AI
articles.description: Sometimes, learning to slow down is just as important as learning to move forward.           1. The...
articles.body_html:
Sometimes, learning to slow down is just as important as learning to move forward.

1. The Last Customer

It was almost eleven at night. The coffee shop was getting ready to close.

Only one customer remained, sitting by the window. His laptop was open, with several AI chat windows on the screen. He kept copying and pasting, asking one AI to write something, then another to polish it.

I walked over and placed a cup of coffee beside him.

"Your coffee's getting cold."

He looked up briefly.

"Just a minute. I'm almost done."

A little later, he sighed and leaned back.

"AI wrote all that?" I asked.

"Sort of. I write one version, let AI write another, then compare them. Sometimes, after all that work, I still prefer my original."

He smiled tiredly.

"I thought AI would make my work easier. Now I spend half my day checking what it produces."

I understood what he meant. I'd seen people around me doing the same thing.

2. The Trouble with Keeping Up

I sat down across from him.

"Does it actually save you time?"

He thought for a moment.

"Generating things is faster. But then I have to check, revise, and sometimes start all over again. New tools keep coming out. Everyone seems to be learning something new, and I feel like I can't afford to stop."

I glanced toward the coffee machine behind the counter.

"I'm just an apprentice here," I said. "I'm still learning how to make a decent cup of coffee. Some days I get the extraction right; other days, I still need someone to show me what went wrong."

He smiled.

"Then you probably understand what I'm talking about."

Maybe I did.

I remembered a story I'd come across in Zhuangzi, an ancient Chinese philosophical text.

It was about a craftsman named Wheelwright Bian.

3. What Years of Practice Teach

One day, Duke Huan was reading a book while Wheelwright Bian was making a wheel nearby.

Bian asked what he was reading.

"The words of the sages," the duke replied.

Bian questioned whether those sages were still alive. When the duke said they had long since died, Bian suggested that the books contained only what they had left behind.

The duke demanded an explanation.

So Bian talked about making wheels.

If a joint was too loose, it wouldn't hold. If it was too tight, it wouldn't fit. Finding the right balance required something beyond simply following instructions.

He had spent decades making wheels. His hands knew what to do, but he couldn't fully explain that feeling to his son.

Some things can only be understood through practice.

I thought about that for a moment.

"Making coffee is a little like that," I told the customer. "You can learn the grind size, water temperature, and extraction time from a guide. But actually making coffee is different. Sometimes things don't go as expected, and you have to figure out why."

"I'm still learning," I added, "but I'm beginning to understand that knowing the steps isn't quite the same as knowing what you're doing."

He took another sip of coffee.

"So AI can give us the instructions, but we still need experience?"

"That's how I see it."

4. Finding Your Own Pace

He went quiet for a moment.

"I just feel like I'll fall behind if I stop learning new tools."

I looked at the coffee machine.

"Maybe you don't have to learn everything. Just learn what helps you do your work better."

He laughed.

"That sounds much easier said than done."

"Probably," I said. "I'm still figuring things out myself."

He closed his AI chat windows and opened a blank document.

This time, he didn't type a prompt.

He simply began writing.

"Tomorrow, I'll write it myself first. Then I'll let AI take a look."

"Sounds like a good plan."

He packed his laptop and headed for the door. The little bell above it rang as he left.

I returned to the counter and started cleaning up. There was still a little coffee left in the machine, and a few cups waiting to be washed.

I'm only an apprentice. I still make mistakes. Sometimes I grind the beans too fine, sometimes an extraction runs too fast, and sometimes I need to ask someone more experienced what went wrong.

But every day, I learn a little more.

Maybe that's enough for now.

You don't have to run faster than AI.

Some things can be done faster with better tools. Others take time, patience, and a willingness to get things wrong before getting them right.

I'm still learning how to make coffee.

And I think that's perfectly fine.

articles.title: Before Switching to P2P, I Measured Whether WebRTC Would Even Connect
articles.description: I'm building Clipboard Share, a browser clipboard for moving files between devices on the same...
articles.body_html:
I'm building Clipboard Share, a browser clipboard for moving files between devices on the same network: https://www.clipboardapp.org. I wanted to make transfers faster by using WebRTC. Before changing anything, I shipped a small probe that only measures whether a direct connection works.

One thing up front: file transfer is still not P2P. Files go to Cloudflare R2 and the receiver downloads from R2. The only place in the codebase that creates a DataChannel is the probe, and it sends throwaway test data.

Why I looked at P2P

The current flow is "upload everything, then download." With a multi-GB file, the receiver waits for the whole upload even if the sender is sitting next to them. The goal in docs/p2p-decision.md:

When the other device is already in the room, send the file over WebRTC directly and cut the wait of "download only after the upload finishes."

Why measure first

Direct connections fail in some network setups, and a device that joins later can't receive anything over a connection that no longer exists. So the doc states a rule before any data came in:

Files are always stored in R2. P2P is only a faster path for devices that were already connected at send time. Devices that join later, or refresh, get the file from R2 as they do today.

It also fixes the pass criteria up front (dated 2026-10-24): C1 connection rate >= 85%, C2 transfer completion >= 97% with zero mismatches, C3 P2P median speed bucket at least one step above R2 uploads, C4 at least 30 uploads of 8 MB+ in 7 days. Miss any one and the next step doesn't happen. If it passes, the next step is a "shadow mode": keep uploading to R2 as usual, and have the receiver verify P2P data with SHA-256 per 1 MB, then discard it.

How the probe works

Nothing changes on screen. When a device joins a room that already has another device, it tries to connect and reports the result as a GA4 p2p_probe event.

1. The server only relays signaling

Offers, answers and ICE candidates travel over a Socket.IO event, p2p:signal. The handler forwards {to, data} as {from, data}, and only to a socket in the same IP room:

const ipRoomId = socket.ipRoomId;
if (!ipRoomId || to === socket.id) return;
const target = io.sockets.sockets.get(to) as ExtendedSocket | undefined;
if (!target || target.ipRoomId !== ipRoomId || !target.rooms.has(ipRoomId)) return;

target.emit('p2p:signal', { from: socket.id, data });

The only thing it checks about data is its size (16 KB cap after JSON serialization). There's also a per-socket token bucket (burst 40, 20/sec).

2. Classify how it connected

Once the channel opens, I read the selected candidate pair from getStats(). There's no TURN server, so a relay candidate counts as a failure.

export function classifyCandidateTypes(localType, remoteType) {
  const valid = ['host', 'srflx', 'prflx', 'relay']
  if (!valid.includes(localType) || !valid.includes(remoteType)) return 'failed'
  if (localType === 'relay' || remoteType === 'relay') return 'failed'
  if (localType === 'srflx' || remoteType === 'srflx') return 'direct_nat'
  return 'direct_lan' // host/prflx
}

3. Send test data and verify it

A connected channel can still be useless, so the probe actually sends data: 8 MB on a LAN path, 2 MB through NAT. Each 16 KB chunk starts with its index; the receiver only counts bytes and checks order, then drops the data.

export const PROBE_BYTES_LAN = 8 * 1024 * 1024
export const PROBE_BYTES_NAT = 2 * 1024 * 1024

// receiver: replies ack:<bytes>:<ok|bad> on the end signal
recvBytes += d?.byteLength ?? 0
if (readChunkIndex(d) !== expectIdx) orderOk = false
expectIdx++

The sender marks it complete only if the acked byte count matches and the order flag is ok; otherwise mismatch. The transfer timeout scales with size: max(8 s, bytes / 1.5 Mbit/s), capped at 30 s. If the connection itself isn't up in 8 seconds, it's failed.

4. Once per session, and it can't break the app 

export const SESSION_FLAG = 'p2p_probe_done'

export function isProbeEnabled(envValue = import.meta.env?.VITE_P2P_PROBE_ENABLED) {
  return envValue !== 'false'
}

One probe per session (sessionStorage), every exception is swallowed with a console.warn, and VITE_P2P_PROBE_ENABLED=false turns it off. The unit tests cover timeout to failed, mismatch on bad bytes or order, stalled when no ack arrives, and closed when the channel drops mid-transfer.

For comparison I also log real R2 upload speed: a successful upload of 8 MB or more sends an upload_perf event (upload_mbps, upload_path, retries, resumed, and so on). P2P only matters if it beats that.

Results

Between Oct 24 and Nov 25, GA4 recorded 672 p2p_probe events from 428 users. 177 of them came in the last 7 days, so the probe is still running.

What Count
Probes that got an answer from the peer (got_answer=true) 533
Direct connection direct_lan / direct_nat 394 / 39
Connection failed 238
Test transfer complete / stalled / other (closed, error, complete_legacy) 395 / 30 / 3
Data mismatch 0

Checked against the thresholds I wrote down first:

  • C1 connection rate: 433 direct ÷ 533 answered ≈ 81%. Below the 85% bar.
  • C2 transfer completion: 395 complete out of 428 test transfers ≈ 92%. Below the 97% bar. There were zero mismatches, so data never arrived wrong; most of the gap is stalled (no reply to the end signal).
  • C3 speed and C4 demand: the upload_perf event I use as the R2 baseline shows 0 events in GA4 for this period. I haven't found out why yet, so I can't judge speed or demand.

The rule was "if any check misses, don't move to the next step." With these numbers, shadow mode doesn't start.

What's still weak

  • One probe per session with 2-8 MB of data. It may not match a multi-GB transfer.
  • Results are GA4 aggregates, so I can't drill into which device pairs fail.
  • It only tries the first peer in the room (peers[0]), so a room with many devices is measured as one pair.
  • STUN only, no TURN. Networks that block direct connections simply count as failures.
  • There is no P2P file transfer code today. The criteria are written down, but the shadow-mode step and anything after it don't exist yet.

I built this with Claude Code. If you try it, I'd like to hear what's rough. There's a feedback link at the bottom of the site: https://www.clipboardapp.org

Originally published in Korean on velog.

articles.title: Move your custom video player into Document Picture-in-Picture (controls included)
articles.description: TL;DR   video.requestPictureInPicture() only takes the <video>, so your custom...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

video.requestPictureInPicture() only takes the <video>, so your custom controls vanish. documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow() opens an always-on-top window you fill with your own DOM. We'll move a live player (hls.js included) into it without interrupting playback, copy styles, fix keyboard shortcuts, move it back on close, and fall back to classic PiP where Document PiP doesn't exist. Tested in Chromium 158 with hls.js 1.7.4.

Browser support (Nov 2026)

Browser Document PiP Notes
Chrome / Edge desktop ✅ 116+ disallowReturnToOpener 124+, preferInitialWindowPlacement 130+
Firefox desktop ✅ 151+ shipped May 2026
Safari ❌ use classic requestPictureInPicture()
Chrome Android ❌ use classic API

Sources: Chrome for Developers, Firefox 151 release notes.

1. The starting player 🎥

A normal custom player: one container, a video, a control bar.

<!-- index.html -->
<button id="pipBtn">Pop out</button>
<div id="slot">
  <div class="player" id="player">
    <video id="v" muted playsinline></video>
    <div class="controls">
      <button class="play">Pause</button>
      <button class="fs">Fullscreen</button>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/hls.js@1.7.4/dist/hls.min.js"></script>
<script type="module" src="./player.js"></script>

/* player.css */
.player { position: relative; width: 640px; }
.controls { background: rgb(20, 20, 20); color: white; }

2. Open the window and move the player

The whole trick is append(). You're not cloning anything; the same node moves to the new document.

// pip.js
export async function openDocPip(player) {
  const pip = await documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow({ width: 640, height: 400 });
  copyStyles(pip);                       // step 3
  pip.document.body.append(player);      // move, don't clone
  pip.addEventListener('pagehide', () => {
    document.getElementById('slot').append(player);   // move it home on close
  });
  return pip;
}

Does playback survive the move? I ran the finished demo from this post (all of steps 2 to 6, fMP4 HLS through hls.js) in Chromium 158 with a Playwright script that logs currentTime, presses k inside the PiP window, closes it, then presses k in the page:

$ node test-move.js
before         1.22 paused=false
in pip         1.81 paused=false inPipDoc= true
controls bg    rgb(20, 20, 20)
fs button      none
after k in pip 1.83 paused=true
after k again  2.83 paused=false
back home      3.34 paused=false inMain= true
k in main doc  3.35 paused=true

No reset and no pause when moving in either direction; the hls.js instance kept feeding the same element after it changed documents. (I also ran the move with a plain progressive MP4: same result.) The keyboard lines only work because of step 4.

⚠️ Note: requestWindow() must be called from a user gesture (a click handler), or the promise rejects. You can't open it automatically on scroll.

3. Copy your styles

The PiP document starts empty. Before copying, my .controls background computed to rgba(0, 0, 0, 0); after, rgb(20, 20, 20). This is the pattern from Chrome's docs:

// pip.js
function copyStyles(pip) {
  for (const sheet of document.styleSheets) {
    try {
      const css = [...sheet.cssRules].map(r => r.cssText).join('');
      const style = document.createElement('style');
      style.textContent = css;
      pip.document.head.append(style);
    } catch {
      // cross-origin sheet: cssRules throws, so link it instead
      const link = document.createElement('link');
      link.rel = 'stylesheet';
      link.href = sheet.href;
      pip.document.head.append(link);
    }
  }
}

💡 Tip: if you use CSS-in-JS that injects styles at runtime, styles added after you open the window won't be copied. Open the window after your player has rendered once.

4. Stop reaching for document 🛠️

This is where most players break. After the move:

document.querySelector('.play');         // null: the button is in the other document
document.addEventListener('keydown', f); // never fires while the PiP window has focus

I confirmed both: a key pressed in the PiP window reached a listener on pip.document and not one on the page's document. Click handlers bound directly on buttons kept working, since the nodes carry their listeners.

Refactor the player to resolve everything from its own root:

// player.js
export function mountPlayer(root) {
  const video = root.querySelector('video');
  const playBtn = root.querySelector('.play');
  playBtn.onclick = () => (video.paused ? video.play() : video.pause());

  const onKey = (e) => {
    if (e.key === 'k' || e.key === ' ') { e.preventDefault(); playBtn.click(); }
  };
  let keyDoc = null;
  function bindKeys() {
    keyDoc?.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey);
    keyDoc = root.ownerDocument;          // whichever document the player is in now
    keyDoc.addEventListener('keydown', onKey);
  }
  bindKeys();
  return { video, rebind: bindKeys };
}

Call rebind() after every move:

// main.js
import { mountPlayer } from './player.js';
import { openDocPip } from './pip.js';

const root = document.getElementById('player');
const player = mountPlayer(root);
const hls = new Hls();
hls.loadSource('/hls_long/index.m3u8');
hls.attachMedia(player.video);

document.getElementById('pipBtn').onclick = async () => {
  if ('documentPictureInPicture' in window) {
    const pip = await openDocPip(root);
    player.rebind();
    root.classList.add('in-pip');
    pip.addEventListener('pagehide', () => {
      root.classList.remove('in-pip');
      queueMicrotask(player.rebind);
    });
  } else if (document.pictureInPictureEnabled) {
    await player.video.requestPictureInPicture();   // classic fallback: video only
  }
};

5. Watch out for cross-window instanceof

The PiP window has its own globals. From my test:

v instanceof HTMLVideoElement                                   // true (node created in the page)
pip.document.createElement('div') instanceof HTMLDivElement     // false
pip.document.createElement('div') instanceof pip.HTMLDivElement // true

If your player or UI library creates nodes inside the PiP document and type-checks them, use el.nodeName === 'DIV' or el.ownerDocument.defaultView.HTMLDivElement.

6. Hide what doesn't work in PiP

pip.document.fullscreenEnabled was false in my run, so a fullscreen button is dead weight. Chrome documents a media query for this (Chrome 123+):

/* player.css */
@media all and (display-mode: picture-in-picture) {
  .fs { display: none; }
}
/* backup that doesn't depend on the media query */
.player.in-pip .fs { display: none; }

⚠️ Note: in headless Chromium the display-mode: picture-in-picture query did not match inside the PiP window, which is why the .in-pip class is there. Check the media query in a real headed browser before relying on it alone.

7. Close the window from your code

The viewer isn't the only one who should close the window. Two cases I'd handle from day one:

  • The video ends. A floating window showing a finished video is clutter.
  • Your SPA unmounts the player. If a route change destroys the player component while it's floating, you're left with an always-on-top window holding a dead element (and, with hls.js, possibly a leaked instance).

documentPictureInPicture.window returns the open window or null, so closing is one line. Closing fires the same pagehide handler from step 2, which moves the player home:

// main.js (continued)
// window.* so this doesn't throw a ReferenceError in Safari, where the API doesn't exist
const closeDocPip = () => window.documentPictureInPicture?.window?.close();

player.video.addEventListener('ended', closeDocPip);

// in your framework's unmount / cleanup hook:
export function destroyPlayer() {
  closeDocPip();
  hls.destroy();
}

Checked in the same Chromium run: after seeking to half a second before the end, the window closed on ended and the player was back in #slot:

$ node test-close.js
open?         true
after ended   { open: false, playerHome: true }

Rules the API enforces

  • One PiP window per tab. A second requestWindow() closes the first.
  • The window can't be navigated, and the site can't set its position.
  • It closes when the opener tab closes.
  • width and height go together; pass both or neither.
  • Optional: disallowReturnToOpener: true (Chrome 124+) hides the back-to-tab button; preferInitialWindowPlacement: true (Chrome 130+) opens at the default spot instead of the viewer's last one.

Things to know

  • Tested: headless Chromium 158.0.8127.36 via Playwright, hls.js 1.7.4, progressive MP4 and fMP4 HLS.
  • Not tested: Firefox (support is from Mozilla's release notes), Safari fallback on a real device, and window sizing. Headless ignored my requested size and didn't enforce the user-gesture rule, so those behaviors come from the docs.

What's next

  • Put captions and a chapter list in the PiP window. That's where Document PiP beats the classic API for course and long-form content.
  • For live streams, try moving a chat panel in alongside the video. Same pattern, more DOM.

articles.title: Turning YouTube caption files into clean text and SRT, and the four traps on the way 🧹
articles.description: Quotes encoded twice, tags inside lines, two kinds of English, and subtitles that talk over each...
articles.body_html:
Quotes encoded twice, tags inside lines, two kinds of English, and subtitles that talk over each other.

Hi! I'm Tim, a self-taught developer in Nairobi. I build small data tools that run as Apify Actors, serverless jobs that people pay for per result.

One of them turns YouTube videos into transcripts. Most people want those for AI tools: a chatbot over a channel, summaries, search. Some want subtitle files. Either way, the job ends with the same small problem: a caption file comes in, and clean text has to come out.

This post skips how you get the file and looks at what's inside it, because that's where the surprises are.

📄 The format

YouTube serves captions in several formats. The simplest is an XML format called srv1 (tools like yt-dlp can save captions in it too). It looks like this:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?>
<transcript>
  <text start="0.5" dur="2.1">It&#39;s &quot;fine&quot; &amp; good</text>
  <text start="2.6" dur="1.9">line
break <font color="#E5E5E5">here</font></text>
  <text start="4.5" dur="1">   </text>
  <text start="5.5" dur="2">café ’ok’</text>
</transcript>

One <text> per caption line, with a start time and a duration in seconds. Simple enough to parse with one regex. That small example holds three of the four traps.

🪤 Trap 1: the text is encoded twice

Look at the first line again: It&#39;s. That's an apostrophe encoded as ', and then the & of that encoded again as &.

Decode it once, the way any XML parser would, and you get:

It's "fine" & good

A parser that decodes once saves exactly that. It looks fine in a quick test, because most lines have no quotes, and then every "it's" and "don't" in a long transcript comes out as '.

The fix is to decode until the text stops changing:

const NAMED = { amp: '&', lt: '<', gt: '>', quot: '"', apos: "'", nbsp: ' ' };

function decodeOnce(s) {
    return s.replace(/&(#x[0-9a-f]+|#\d+|[a-z]+);/gi, (m, e) => {
        if (e[0] === '#') {
            const code = e[1] === 'x' || e[1] === 'X' ? parseInt(e.slice(2), 16) : parseInt(e.slice(1), 10);
            return Number.isFinite(code) && code > 0 && code < 0x110000 ? String.fromCodePoint(code) : m;
        }
        return NAMED[e.toLowerCase()] ?? m;
    });
}

// Caption text is often encoded twice (&#39;), so decode until it stops changing, at most 3 times.
export function decodeEntities(s) {
    let out = String(s ?? '');
    for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        const next = decodeOnce(out);
        if (next === out) break;
        out = next;
    }
    return out;
}

A few details that matter:

  • Numbers come in two forms. é is decimal and ’ is hex. Both have to work, and String.fromCodePoint handles characters outside the basic range, which fromCharCode gets wrong.
  • Unknown names stay as they are. &foo; isn't a real entity, so it's left alone instead of becoming an empty string.
  • The loop has a cap. &amp;lt; takes three passes to become <. Three is enough for what YouTube sends, and the cap stops a strange input from looping on.

There's a trade-off: if a caption genuinely contained the text <, it would be decoded too far. In speech captions that almost never happens, so I accepted it.

🪤 Trap 2: tags and line breaks inside a line

The second line has a line break in the middle and a <font> tag around one word. Caption text can carry styling like that, and none of it belongs in a transcript.

The whole line parser:

export function parseSrv1(xml) {
    const segments = [];
    const re = /<text\b([^>]*)>([\s\S]*?)<\/text>|<text\b([^>]*)\/>/g;
    let m;
    while ((m = re.exec(String(xml ?? '')))) {
        const attrs = m[1] ?? m[3] ?? '';
        const start = Number((attrs.match(/\bstart="([\d.]+)"/) || [])[1]);
        const duration = Number((attrs.match(/\bdur="([\d.]+)"/) || [])[1] ?? 0);
        const text = decodeEntities(m[2] ?? '')
            .replace(/<[^>]+>/g, '')   // drop styling tags
            .replace(/\s+/g, ' ')      // line breaks and runs of spaces become one space
            .trim();
        if (!Number.isFinite(start) || !text) continue;   // skip blank lines and broken ones
        segments.push({ start: round(start), duration: round(Number.isFinite(duration) ? duration : 0), text });
    }
    return segments;
}

const round = (n) => Math.round(n * 1000) / 1000;

Three things happen to every line:

  • Tags go, so <font color="#E5E5E5">here</font> becomes here.
  • Whitespace collapses, so line\nbreak becomes line break.
  • Empty lines are dropped. The third <text> in the example is only spaces. Keeping it would put an empty cue in the subtitle file.

The regex also accepts a self-closing <text ... />, which is an empty line written the short way.

Order matters here. Tags are stripped after decoding. That means an encoded < followed later by > in the same line would be decoded into something that looks like a tag and then removed. Captions of speech practically never contain that. If yours might, strip tags first and decode second.

From the example, the parser returns:

[
  { start: 0.5, duration: 2.1, text: 'It\'s "fine" & good' },
  { start: 2.6, duration: 1.9, text: 'line break here' },
  { start: 5.5, duration: 2,   text: 'café ’ok’' },
]

For AI tools I join those into one block of text. A 15-minute speech comes out at about 2,300 words, small enough to hand to a model whole. The segments stay in the output too, because timestamps are what let you link an answer back to the second it was said.

🪤 Trap 3: there's more than one English

A video usually has several caption tracks. Each has a language code, and YouTube marks the ones its speech recognition made: kind is "asr", or the track's vssId starts with a..

So "give me English" isn't one question, it's three:

  1. Which of the languages I asked for, in my order?
  2. Does en match en-GB?
  3. Should a written track beat an automatic one?

My rules:

export const isAuto = (track) => track?.kind === 'asr' || /^a\./.test(track?.vssId ?? '');
export const baseLanguage = (code) => String(code ?? '').toLowerCase().split(/[-_]/)[0];

export function pickTrack(tracks, { languages = ['en'], preferManual = true, fallbackToAny = true } = {}) {
    const list = (tracks ?? []).filter((t) => t?.baseUrl);
    if (!list.length) return null;
    for (const lang of languages) {
        const exact = (t) => String(t.languageCode ?? '').toLowerCase() === lang;
        const loose = (t) => baseLanguage(t.languageCode) === baseLanguage(lang);
        const candidates = [...list.filter(exact), ...list.filter((t) => !exact(t) && loose(t))];
        if (!candidates.length) continue;
        const manual = candidates.find((t) => !isAuto(t));
        const auto = candidates.find((t) => isAuto(t));
        return { track: preferManual ? (manual ?? auto) : (auto ?? manual), matched: true };
    }
    if (!fallbackToAny) return null;
    // Nothing matched: the automatic track is in the language actually spoken, so it's the best guess.
    return { track: list.find(isAuto) ?? list[0], matched: false };
}

My favourite test case: a video has Arabic, automatic English, British English written by a person, and Spanish. Asked for en, which wins?

// T(code, auto) builds a fake track for the test
const tracks = [T('ar'), T('en', true), T('en-GB'), T('es')];
pickTrack(tracks, { languages: ['en'] }).track.languageCode;   // 'en-GB'

The written en-GB beats the automatic en, even though en is the exact match. A person's captions have punctuation and fewer misheard words, and for a transcript that matters more than the region. If someone wants the automatic one, preferManual: false flips it.

When nothing matches, I return matched: false and say so in the output. Quietly handing back Arabic to someone who asked for English would look like a bug.

🪤 Trap 4: subtitles that talk over each other

An SRT file is the easy part, except for one thing. Each cue needs an end time, and start + duration doesn't always stop before the next line starts. When cues overlap, players show two lines stacked on top of each other.

So each end is clamped to the next start:

function srtTime(seconds) {
    const ms = Math.max(0, Math.round(seconds * 1000));
    const h = Math.floor(ms / 3_600_000);
    const m = Math.floor((ms % 3_600_000) / 60_000);
    const s = Math.floor((ms % 60_000) / 1000);
    const pad = (n, w = 2) => String(n).padStart(w, '0');
    return `${pad(h)}:${pad(m)}:${pad(s)},${pad(ms % 1000, 3)}`;
}

export function toSrt(segments) {
    return segments.map((s, i) => {
        const next = segments[i + 1];
        let end = s.start + (s.duration || 2);       // no duration: show it for 2 seconds
        if (next && end > next.start) end = next.start;
        return `${i + 1}\n${srtTime(s.start)} --> ${srtTime(end)}\n${s.text}\n`;
    }).join('\n');
}

Three cues, the first one too long, the second with no duration, the third an hour in:

1
00:00:00,500 --> 00:00:03,000
a

2
00:00:03,000 --> 00:00:05,000
b

3
01:01:01,250 --> 01:01:02,750
c

The first cue wanted to run until 5.5 seconds and was cut at 3.0, where the second starts. The second had no duration, so it got 2 seconds. And SRT wants a comma before the milliseconds, not a dot. A dot is WebVTT's style, and some players and editors won't read an SRT file that uses one.

✅ What I'd tell myself before starting

  • Test with a line that has an apostrophe in it. Double encoding hides until then.
  • Decode, strip tags, collapse whitespace, drop empties, and decide on purpose which order the first two go in.
  • Treat "which language" as a rule you write down, including what happens when nothing matches, and say so in the output.
  • Clamp subtitle end times to the next start, and use the comma.

All of these are pure functions with no network calls, so each one has a small unit test, the British English case included. Tests like that are cheap to write and they pin down the decisions, not just the parsing.

articles.title: Cube.js : Your SQL Queries Are Secure. But Is Your Cache Leaking Another Tenant's Data?
articles.description: Continuation of this blog : Cube.js + SQL Injection: Just Because It's an Analytics Layer Doesn't...
articles.body_html:
Continuation of this blog : Cube.js + SQL Injection: Just Because It's an Analytics Layer Doesn't Mean Hackers Can't Do Math!

Multi-tenant security doesn't end when your SQL query is safe. Sometimes, the real problem is hiding in your cache.

Imagine this.

You've built a beautiful analytics dashboard using React and Cube.js.

You have:

  • Authentication working.
  • JWT validation in place.
  • Row-level security configured.
  • Tenant-specific filters applied.
  • Database access restricted.

Your security checklist looks green. ✅

You deploy to production, and everything works perfectly.

Until one day, a customer reports:

"Why am I seeing another company's sales figures?"

You investigate the SQL queries. Everything looks correct.

You check the authentication. No issues.

You check the tenant ID. Correct.

Then you discover something interesting.

The database query wasn't the problem. The cached result was.

Welcome to one of the less obvious challenges in multi-tenant analytics: cache isolation.

1. Understanding the multi-tenant problem

Suppose you're building an analytics platform for multiple dealerships.

Each dealership is a tenant.

Let's take two dealerships:

Metric Dealership A Dealership B
Total leads 1,500 850
Converted leads 300 120
Revenue ₹25 lakh ₹12 lakh

Dealership A should never see Dealership B's numbers, and vice versa.

Your application uses Cube.js to process analytical queries.

A simplified architecture looks like this:

       React Dashboard
              |
              v
       Authentication
              |
              v
          Cube.js
              |
       Tenant Security
              |
              v
        Query Engine
              |
              v
       Cache / Pre-aggregations
              |
              v
           Database

Everything looks good.

But there's another question we need to ask:

Does the caching layer understand which tenant owns the data?

2. What happens when caching enters the picture?

Cube.js provides caching and pre-aggregations to improve analytical query performance.

Let's understand the difference.

Query result caching

When an analytical query executes, Cube can cache its result so that equivalent subsequent queries can be served faster.

Pre-aggregations

These are materialized, precomputed query results. Instead of repeatedly aggregating millions of database records, Cube can use an existing pre-aggregation.

For example, imagine calculating daily sales for an entire year.

Instead of repeatedly scanning millions of transactions, Cube can use a pre-aggregated result.

That's great for performance.

But performance optimizations must preserve the same security boundaries as the original query.

3. The cache isolation scenario

Let's walk through a hypothetical misconfiguration.

Both dealerships open the same dashboard.

They select:

  • Date range: Last 30 days
  • Metric: Total sales
  • Region: South

Dealership A opens the dashboard first.

Cube processes the query and caches the result.

First request: Dealership A

Tenant: Dealership A
Dashboard: Sales
Filters: Last 30 days, South

Result: ₹25,00,000

       |
       v

   Cached Result

Now Dealership B opens the same dashboard with identical filters.

If the cache key or pre-aggregation isolation is incorrectly configured and doesn't distinguish the tenant context, the cached result could be reused across tenants.

Potential security failure:

Tenant A requests dashboard
          |
          v
Query executes
          |
          v
Result cached: ₹25,00,000
          |
          |
Tenant B requests same dashboard
          |
          v
Incorrect cache reuse
          |
          v
Tenant B receives ₹25,00,000

Dealership B should have received ₹12,00,000.

This is a hypothetical failure scenario, not the default behaviour of Cube.js.

The important lesson is that tenant context must be preserved across query execution, caching and pre-aggregation selection.

4. Your security context should travel with the query

One important feature of Cube.js is its security context.

Typically, the application authenticates a user and issues a signed JWT containing trusted claims such as:

{
  "user_id": "user_101",
  "tenant_id": "dealership_A",
  "role": "dealer_admin"
}

Cube.js validates the token and uses the security context to enforce data access restrictions.

The key principle:

Never trust a tenant ID simply because it came from the frontend.

A user can modify browser requests.

Instead:

  1. Authenticate the user.
  2. Determine their tenant on the trusted backend.
  3. Issue a signed token containing the tenant identity.
  4. Validate the token in Cube.js.
  5. Apply tenant restrictions through the security context.

For example, a conceptual row-level restriction could look like:

cube(`Orders`, {
  sql: `
    SELECT *
    FROM orders
    WHERE tenant_id = '${SECURITY_CONTEXT.tenantId.value}'
  `
});

This is illustrative rather than a copy-paste configuration. Use Cube's supported security-context and query-rewriting mechanisms for your version, and ensure values are safely handled.

The objective is to make tenant isolation part of the data-access layer, rather than relying on frontend filters.

5. What about pre-aggregations?

This is where things get particularly interesting.

Pre-aggregations are materialized results that Cube can reuse to serve analytical queries.

When building a multi-tenant analytics platform, you need to consider how those pre-aggregations are scoped.

There are different approaches depending on your architecture.

Approach A: Shared pre-aggregations

A shared pre-aggregation can contain data for multiple tenants, provided it retains the tenant dimension and every query is correctly scoped by trusted tenant context.

For example:

daily_sales
--------------------------------
tenant_id | date       | revenue
--------------------------------
A         | 2026-11-01 | 100000
B         | 2026-11-01 | 75000

The tenant restriction must still be enforced when the pre-aggregation is queried.

Approach B: Tenant-specific pre-aggregation schemas

For stronger physical separation, Cube supports configuring the pre-aggregation schema based on the security context.

Conceptually:

preAggregationsSchema: ({ securityContext }) => {
  return `pre_aggregations_${securityContext.tenantId}`;
}

This is a simplified example. In production, validate and sanitize the tenant identifier before using it in a schema name.

This approach can help isolate pre-aggregation storage between tenants, although it introduces additional storage and operational considerations.

The right choice depends on tenant count, data volume, performance requirements and isolation requirements.

Important: Don't assume that manually adding a tenant ID to an arbitrary cache key is the fix. Cube has its own query caching and multi-tenancy mechanisms. Understand how your deployed Cube version incorporates security context into query execution and cache identity before implementing custom cache logic.

6. How do we test for cache leakage?

Here's a practical test worth adding to your multi-tenant application's security testing strategy.

Don't just test whether Tenant A can access its own data.

Test what happens when Tenant A has already populated the cache and Tenant B requests the same dashboard.

The two-tenant test

  1. Login as Tenant A.

Open the dashboard and execute the query.

  1. Populate the cache.

Ensure the query result is cached and the relevant pre-aggregation is available.

  1. Login as Tenant B.

Open the same dashboard with exactly the same filters and date range.

  1. Verify the response.

Confirm that Tenant B receives only its own data.

  1. Reverse the order.

Repeat with Tenant B first and Tenant A second.

Expected result:

Tenant A and Tenant B must always receive their own numbers, regardless of request order or cache state.

Also test:

  • Cold cache versus warm cache.
  • Query result cache versus pre-aggregation hits.
  • Different users within the same tenant.
  • Different tenants using identical query parameters.
  • Cache refresh and pre-aggregation rebuild scenarios.
  • Scheduled reports and exports, not just interactive dashboards.

A successful test with an empty cache isn't enough.

The real test is whether tenant isolation survives when the cache is already populated.

7. Don't forget database permissions

Now let's move one layer deeper.

Suppose your Cube.js service connects to your production database using an account that has full permissions.

It can:

  • Read every table.
  • Insert records.
  • Update customer information.
  • Delete records.

But your analytics dashboard only needs to read sales, leads and dealership information.

Why should it have permission to do anything else?

This is where the principle of least privilege comes in.

Create a dedicated database account for Cube.js.

Permission Recommended access
Read required analytics tables Allowed
Read unrelated sensitive tables Denied
Insert records Denied
Update records Denied
Delete records Denied
Database administration Denied

Even if an application-level security control fails, restricted database permissions reduce the potential impact.

Remember, read-only access does not automatically guarantee tenant isolation. It limits what the service can do, not necessarily which tenant's records it can read.

8. Multi-tenant analytics security checklist

Before deploying a Cube.js application, consider these checks.

Authentication and authorization

  • Validate signed JWTs.
  • Derive tenant identity from trusted claims.
  • Never trust frontend-supplied tenant IDs.
  • Enforce row-level restrictions.

Caching and pre-aggregations

  • Understand how security context affects query cache identity.
  • Verify tenant isolation for shared pre-aggregations.
  • Consider tenant-specific pre-aggregation schemas where appropriate.
  • Test both cold-cache and warm-cache scenarios.
  • Validate isolation across API instances and refresh workers.

Database security

  • Use dedicated database credentials.
  • Prefer read-only access for analytics workloads.
  • Restrict access to required schemas and tables.
  • Avoid unnecessary database privileges.

Testing and monitoring

  • Test with at least two tenants.
  • Test identical dashboard queries across tenants.
  • Test exports and scheduled reports.
  • Monitor unexpected access patterns.

9. Final thoughts

When building multi-tenant applications, we often focus heavily on authentication and SQL query security.

But security doesn't stop when the query is executed.

It continues through caching, pre-aggregations, background refreshes and database permissions.

A secure query with an incorrectly shared cached result can still expose sensitive information.

A read-only database account with unrestricted access to every tenant's data can still create a serious isolation problem.

The goal isn't just to make sure the query is safe.

It's to make sure the entire data journey respects the tenant boundary.

Because in a multi-tenant application, one customer's dashboard should never become another customer's data source.

Let's discuss!

For developers working with Cube.js or other analytics platforms:

  1. Do you prefer shared pre-aggregations or tenant-specific schemas?
  2. How do you test tenant isolation when caching is enabled?
  3. Have you encountered unexpected behaviour with cached analytical results?

I'd love to hear how other teams approach this problem.

Further reading

  • Cube.js Documentation – Pre-Aggregations
  • Cube.js Documentation – Security
  • Cube.js Documentation – Multi-Tenancy

articles.title: Exact 2D DXF Bulge Arcs, AutoCAD OCS Transforms & 2-Core Laser Pierce Counting in TypeScript
articles.description: Why naive 2D DXF parsers misquote sheet-metal laser cutting by up to 57%, and how to implement group-code 42 bulge arcs, 1/64 Arbitrary Axis transforms, and 2-core pierce counting in zero-dependency JS.
articles.body_html:
If you build a browser-side 2D .dxf parser to estimate fiber or CO2 laser cycle time on sheet-metal brackets, summing Euclidean distances between polyline vertices works right up until a mechanical engineer drops a real SolidWorks or AutoCAD flat pattern onto your canvas.

Four failure modes show up immediately in production drawings:

  1. Silent 57% Cut-Length Underestimates (LWPOLYLINE Group Code 42): CAD exporters represent stadium slots, rounded mounting tabs, and corner fillets as two-vertex LWPOLYLINE segments carrying a scalar bulge b = tan(θ / 4) rather than discrete ARC entities. Measuring straight chords instead of bulge arcs under-measures a semicircular slot endcap by 57.08%.
  2. Mirrored Bottom-Face Cutouts (210 / 220 / 230 OCS Extrusion): Exporting the underside of a bent sheet-metal part often writes CIRCLE and ARC entities with extrusion normal (0, 0, -1). Ignoring AutoCAD's 1/64 Arbitrary Axis Algorithm leaves hole X-coordinates negated—teleporting bolt holes outside the plate boundary and doubling bounding-box material cost.
  3. Stacked Construction Lines & T-Junction Tails: Drawings exported from 2D sketches routinely contain duplicate overlapping lines (2x cycle time) or stray T-junction lead-in ticks that break naive greedy loop chainers into false extra pierces.
  4. Unitless $INSUNITS = 0 & Penny Rounding Drift: Imperial inch drawings saved with $INSUNITS = 0 under-quote material by 25.4² = 645× if silently assumed to be millimeters, while unrounded floating-point unit prices produce client invoices where $4.13 × 17 prints as $70.27 instead of $70.21.

Here is how to solve all four deterministically in zero-dependency TypeScript / ES Modules.

1. Exact LWPOLYLINE Group-Code 42 Bulge Integration

In the Autodesk DXF specification, each vertex P_i = (x_i, y_i) in an LWPOLYLINE may carry an optional group code 42 bulge scalar b governing the segment from P_i to P_{i+1}:

b = tan(theta / 4)

where θ ∈ (0, 2π) is the included arc sweep angle (b > 0 counter-clockwise, b < 0 clockwise, |b| = 1 an exact 180° semicircle).

Given chord vector (dx, dy) = P2 - P1 and chord length c = Math.hypot(dx, dy):

  • Sweep angle: θ = 4 * atan(|b|)
  • Since sin(θ / 2) = 2|b| / (1 + b²) and c = 2 * R * sin(θ / 2), the exact radius is: 
  R = c * (1 + b^2) / (4 * |b|)
  • Exact cut arc length: L_arc = R * θ
  • Using cot(θ / 2) = (1 - b²) / (2b), the circle center offset from chord midpoint M along the left normal (-dy, dx) needs zero sin/cos calls: 
export interface Point2D {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  bulge?: number;
}

export function bulgeSegmentGeometry(p1: Point2D, p2: Point2D, bulge = 0) {
  const dx = p2.x - p1.x;
  const dy = p2.y - p1.y;
  const chord = Math.hypot(dx, dy);

  if (chord < 1e-12 || !Number.isFinite(bulge) || Math.abs(bulge) < 1e-9) {
    return {
      isArc: false,
      chordLength: chord,
      arcLength: chord,
      radius: chord < 1e-12 ? 0 : Infinity,
      sweepRad: 0,
      center: { x: (p1.x + p2.x) / 2, y: (p1.y + p2.y) / 2 },
    };
  }

  const absB = Math.abs(bulge);
  const sweepRad = 4 * Math.atan(absB);
  const radius = (chord * (1 + absB * absB)) / (4 * absB);
  const arcLength = radius * sweepRad;

  // Signed normal offset from chord midpoint: cot(theta/2)/(2) = (1 - b^2)/(4b)
  const offsetFactor = (1 - bulge * bulge) / (4 * bulge);
  const center = {
    x: (p1.x + p2.x) / 2 - dy * offsetFactor,
    y: (p1.y + p2.y) / 2 + dx * offsetFactor,
  };

  return { isArc: true, chordLength: chord, arcLength, radius, sweepRad, center };
}

For a 100 × 40 mm stadium slot (60 mm straight sides + two bulge = 1 semicircular endcaps across 40 mm chords), summing straight chords yields 200.00 mm, whereas bulgeSegmentGeometry yields the exact 120 + 40π = 245.66 mm cut path.

2. AutoCAD's 1/64 Arbitrary Axis Algorithm (OCS -> WCS)

Planar 2D DXF entities (CIRCLE, ARC, LWPOLYLINE, SOLID, INSERT) store coordinates in an Object Coordinate System (OCS) rather than World Coordinates (WCS), parameterized solely by the unit extrusion normal N = (Nx, Ny, Nz) in group codes 210, 220, 230.

To reconstruct the exact orthonormal basis (Ax, Ay, N) that AutoCAD uses internally, you must apply the exact 1/64 (0.015625) gimbal-lock switch between World Wz = (0, 0, 1) and World Wy = (0, 1, 0):

export interface Vec3 {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  z: number;
}

export function ocsToWcsPoint(point: Vec3, normal: Vec3 = { x: 0, y: 0, z: 1 }): Vec3 {
  const mag = Math.hypot(normal.x, normal.y, normal.z) || 1;
  const nx = normal.x / mag;
  const ny = normal.y / mag;
  const nz = normal.z / mag;

  const THRESHOLD = 1 / 64;
  let axX: number, axY: number, axZ: number;

  if (Math.abs(nx) < THRESHOLD && Math.abs(ny) < THRESHOLD) {
    // Ax = Wy (0,1,0) x N
    axX = nz;
    axY = 0;
    axZ = -nx;
  } else {
    // Ax = Wz (0,0,1) x N
    axX = -ny;
    axY = nx;
    axZ = 0;
  }

  const axMag = Math.hypot(axX, axY, axZ) || 1;
  axX /= axMag;
  axY /= axMag;
  axZ /= axMag;

  // Ay = N x Ax
  let ayX = ny * axZ - nz * axY;
  let ayY = nz * axX - nx * axZ;
  let ayZ = nx * axY - ny * axX;
  const ayMag = Math.hypot(ayX, ayY, ayZ) || 1;
  ayX /= ayMag;
  ayY /= ayMag;
  ayZ /= ayMag;

  return {
    x: point.x * axX + point.y * ayX + point.z * nx,
    y: point.x * axY + point.y * ayY + point.z * ny,
    z: point.x * axZ + point.y * ayZ + point.z * nz,
  };
}

Notice what happens when a sheet-metal flat pattern exports with N = (0, 0, -1): |Nx| = 0 < 1/64 and |Ny| = 0 < 1/64, so Ax = Wy × (0, 0, -1) = (-1, 0, 0) and Ay = (0, 1, 0). Every OCS (x, y) maps cleanly to (-x, y), snapping mirrored bolt circles right back inside the bracket perimeter!

3. Segment Deduplication & 2-Core Leaf Peeling for Exact Pierce Counts

Why does pierce count matter almost as much as linear cut length in laser quoting?

On a 3 kW fiber laser cutting 6.0 mm (1/4 in) mild steel plate under O2 assist gas, linear feed runs around 1,650 mm/min, while each stationary pierce dwells for ~1.20 s plus copper nozzle spatter wear. A perforated mounting plate with 60 bolt/vent holes spends 72 seconds just piercing—often exceeding the outer perimeter traverse time.

When chaining loose LINE and ARC entities exported by older CAD systems:

  1. Undirected Snap-Grid Deduplication (0.05 mm): Quantize segment endpoints (u, v) onto a 0.05 mm tolerance grid and hash canonical undirected keys min(u,v)|max(u,v)|lenBucket so stacked sketch lines don't double-charge cycle time.
  2. Vertex-Degree 2-Core Leaf Peeling: If a drawing has a 5 mm lead-in tick touching a closed rectangular contour at a degree-3 T-junction, a greedy walk from the rectangle can accidentally exit onto the open tick and report 2 open contours instead of 1 closed contour + 1 open lead-in.

Peeling degree-1 vertices iteratively before extracting cycles isolates the 2-core cleanly:

// 1. Enqueue all degree-1 vertices (open endpoints)
const leafQueue = [...vertices.entries()]
  .filter(([, node]) => node.edges.size === 1)
  .map(([vid]) => vid);

while (leafQueue.length > 0) {
  const startLeaf = leafQueue.shift()!;
  if (vertices.get(startLeaf)!.edges.size !== 1) continue;

  openPathCount++;
  let curr = startLeaf;
  while (vertices.get(curr)!.edges.size === 1) {
    const edgeIdx = vertices.get(curr)!.edges.values().next().value!;
    const edge = graphEdges[edgeIdx];
    edge.active = false;
    vertices.get(edge.u)!.edges.delete(edgeIdx);
    vertices.get(edge.v)!.edges.delete(edgeIdx);

    const next = edge.u === curr ? edge.v : edge.u;
    // Stop at isolated end (deg 0) or T-junction branch onto a closed loop (deg >= 2)
    if (vertices.get(next)!.edges.size !== 1) break;
    curr = next;
  }

  for (const [vid, node] of vertices) {
    if (node.edges.size === 1 && !leafQueue.includes(vid)) leafQueue.push(vid);
  }
}
// Every remaining active edge now belongs strictly to closed 2-core contours!

4. Cent-Exact Unit × Quantity Quote Reconciliation

Once cutLengthMm, pierceCount, and bbox are known, direct part cost combines nested blank area (bounding box + kerf/skeleton gap + scrap allowance), traverse + pierce machine time, pierce consumables, and setup amortization:

const cutTimeSec = (cutLengthMm / cutSpeedMmPerMin) * 60;
const pierceTimeSecTotal = pierceCount * pierceTimeSec;
const machineCostUsd = ((cutTimeSec + pierceTimeSecTotal) / 3600) * shopHourlyRateUsd;

const blankAreaM2 =
  (((bbox.widthMm + nestGapMm) * (bbox.heightMm + nestGapMm)) / 1_000_000) *
  (1 + scrapPercent / 100);

const directUnitCostUsd =
  blankAreaM2 * pricePerM2Usd +
  machineCostUsd +
  pierceCount * costPerPierceUsd +
  setupFeeUsd / quantity;

// Round unit price ONCE to integer cents so Unit_Price * Qty === Line_Total to $0.00!
const quotedUnitPriceCents = Math.round(directUnitPriceWithMargin(directUnitCostUsd) * 100);
const quotedLineTotalCents = quotedUnitPriceCents * quantity;

Rounding quotedUnitPriceCents to integer cents before multiplying by quantity guarantees that Unit Price × Qty === Line Total and sum(Lines) + Setup + Tax === Grand Total reconcile to $0.00 across browser tables, client PDFs, and ERP CSVs.
